title: Brand Identity Design: From Strategy to Visual System
subtitle: Turn brand strategy into logos, color and type systems, guidelines and consistent experiences across channels
description:
A brand identity is far more than a logo. It is a system of strategy, visuals and verbal cues that helps the right people recognize, remember and trust a business. This course follows the path professional identity designers take: defining strategy and positioning, translating personality into visual direction, designing logos that work at every size, and building color, typography, imagery and motion systems with design tokens.

You will then document everything in practical brand guidelines (with a fill-in template), deliver living asset libraries in Figma and Canva, govern consistency across social, web, packaging and partnerships, present work in mockups, and plan refreshes, rebrands and rollouts without losing hard-won recognition. Lessons cover accessibility (WCAG 2.2), trademark basics, creator disclosure and responsible use of AI. Every lesson includes a narrated lecture with worked examples from the UK, US, Pakistan, the UAE and Saudi Arabia.
outcomes: Translate brand strategy (audience, positioning, personality) into a visual direction and creative brief
Design and evaluate logos with a scorecard, and present them in context with mockups
Build a logo system with lockups, clear space, minimum sizes, icon sets and a file pack
Create accessible color and typography systems and hand them off as design tokens
Write practical brand guidelines and deliver living libraries teams and partners can use
Govern consistency across social, web, documents, packaging and partnerships
Plan and roll out a refresh or rebrand while protecting brand equity

lessons.title: What brand identity really is
lessons.body:
### Brand, branding and brand identity

These words are often used interchangeably, but separating them makes your work sharper:

- **Brand** — the perceptions, feelings and expectations people hold about a business, creator or product. It lives in people's heads, and you can only influence it.
- **Branding** — the ongoing work of shaping those perceptions through products, service, communication and experiences.
- **Brand identity** — the tangible, designed system that expresses the brand: name, logo, colors, typography, imagery, voice, patterns, motion, sound and the rules for using them.

A beautiful identity cannot fix a poor product or bad service. What it can do is make a good business easier to recognize, remember, choose and trust.

### What a strong identity does

1. **Recognition** — people identify the brand quickly, even from fragments (a color, a shape, a typeface).
2. **Differentiation** — it looks and sounds different from competitors in the category.
3. **Meaning** — it signals the right personality and quality level to the right audience.
4. **Consistency** — it repeats the same cues across every touchpoint so memory builds over time.
5. **Flexibility** — it works across formats, from a tiny app icon to a shop sign or a vertical video.

Marketing research often discusses **distinctive brand assets** — cues such as colors, shapes, characters, taglines or sounds that people link to a brand. The key idea for designers: an asset only becomes distinctive through consistent, long-term use. Changing your colors every season prevents any of them from becoming yours.

### The brand identity stack

Think of identity work as layers, each depending on the one below:

```
6. Touchpoints        social, website, packaging, signage, merch, email
5. Guidelines         rules, templates, examples, governance
4. Supporting system  imagery, icons, patterns, motion, sound
3. Core visuals       logo, color, typography
2. Verbal identity    name, tagline, voice and tone, key messages
1. Strategy           purpose, audience, positioning, personality, values
```

Most weak identities skip layer 1. The designer jumps straight to logos and colors based on personal taste, and the result has no clear reason to exist.

### Strategy in one page

Before any design work, you should be able to answer these questions:

| Element | Question | Example (a Lahore-based home-baking brand) |
|---|---|---|
| Purpose | Why do we exist beyond profit? | Make celebrations feel homemade, even for busy families |
| Audience | Who exactly are we for? | Working parents ordering for birthdays and Eid gatherings |
| Problem | What do they struggle with? | Bakery cakes feel generic; homemade takes too long |
| Positioning | Why us instead of alternatives? | Home-baked quality with bakery reliability and on-time delivery |
| Personality | If we were a person? | Warm, generous, reliable, a little playful |
| Proof | Why should people believe us? | Real reviews, ingredient transparency, delivery guarantee |

### Identity for creators and personal brands

For creators, the "business" is often a person. The identity still needs a system — but it should amplify the human, not hide them. Typical elements: a consistent color world, one or two typefaces, a recognizable thumbnail or cover style, a signature phrase or intro, and a consistent photo style. The creator's face, voice and viewpoint are usually the strongest distinctive assets.

### Worked example: two identities, same product

Two coffee roasters sell similar beans.

- **Roaster A:** positioned as a premium, craft-focused specialist. Identity: restrained palette of off-white and deep brown, elegant serif wordmark, detailed origin illustrations, calm editorial photography.
- **Roaster B:** positioned as an energetic everyday coffee for students and young professionals. Identity: bold orange and black, chunky sans-serif, playful stickers, bright flash photography.

Neither identity is "better". Each is right for its strategy — and each would be wrong for the other.

### Common mistakes

- Designing before strategy is agreed.
- Copying a successful competitor's look, which makes you blend in.
- Treating the logo as the whole identity.
- Changing visual assets so often that nothing becomes recognizable.

### The chain: strategy → identity → guidelines → experience

Every decision in this course sits somewhere on one chain. If a link is missing, the identity drifts.

| Link | Question it answers | Output |
|---|---|---|
| Strategy | Who are we for, what do we promise, how are we different? | One-page strategy, positioning, personality |
| Identity | How does that look, sound and move? | Logo system, color, type, imagery, voice, motion |
| Guidelines | How does everyone apply it correctly? | Brand guidelines, templates, asset library, tokens |
| Experience | What do people actually encounter? | Posts, packaging, website, service, invoices |
| Feedback | Is it working? | Recognition, consistency audits, customer language |

### Hands-on: the one-page brand strategy (template)

```text
ONE-PAGE BRAND STRATEGY — [brand]            version / date
Purpose:        Why we exist beyond profit (one sentence)
Audience:       Primary audience, in specifics (who, where, what they need)
Problem:        The tension or frustration we solve
Promise:        What people can always expect from us
Positioning:    For [audience] who [need], [brand] is the [category]
                that [difference] because [proof].
Personality:    3 traits + "we are ___ but not ___" ×3
Proof points:   3 facts that make the promise believable
Competitors:    3 names + how we look/sound different
Distinctive assets to build: color? shape? character? sound?
Must never:     2-3 things the brand must never be or do
```

### Where AI helps (and where it doesn't) in brand strategy

AI assistants are useful for summarizing large volumes of reviews or survey answers, clustering customer language, and drafting alternative positioning statements to react to. They are not a substitute for talking to customers, and they tend to produce the same generic adjectives every competitor uses. Anonymize customer data before pasting it into any AI tool, and follow your organization's data policies.

### Before/after: a strategy line that designers can use

| | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Brief | "We want to look modern, trustworthy and premium." | "For busy parents in Lahore who distrust generic baby products, Nano Nest is the baby-care shop that stocks only pediatrician-reviewed brands, because every product passes our three-step review." |
| Designer's reaction | "So… blue and a sans serif?" | "Calm, clinical-but-warm, evidence-led, family-focused — let's explore a soft green with a friendly rounded wordmark and a 'checked' motif." |

(Brand name and details are illustrative.)

### Summary

A brand is perception; an identity is the designed system that shapes it. Build from strategy upward, aim for recognition, differentiation, meaning, consistency and flexibility, and remember that distinctiveness comes from consistent use over time.

Usually they mean all of it, and they don't know where one ends and the next begins. That confusion leads to expensive mistakes, like a beautiful logo that doesn't fix a confusing business, or a rebrand that throws away the one thing customers recognized. In this lecture, you'll learn the difference between brand, branding and brand identity, what a strong identity actually does, the chain from strategy to identity to guidelines, and a one-page strategy template. By the end, you'll know what to design, and why.

lessons.title: Personality, voice and positioning
lessons.body:
### From strategy words to design decisions

"Modern, trustworthy and innovative" appears in countless briefs — and means almost nothing. Every competitor claims the same. This lesson turns vague adjectives into specific, differentiated direction that designers and writers can act on.

### Positioning: the anchor

A classic positioning statement template:

```
For [specific audience]
who [need or problem],
[brand] is the [category / frame of reference]
that [key benefit / point of difference]
because [reason to believe].
```

Example for a UAE-based freelance video editor: "For e-commerce brands in the Gulf who need fast, on-brand product videos, Frame&Cut is the video partner that delivers ready-to-post ads in Arabic and English within 72 hours, because we run a dedicated bilingual editing team with ready-made brand templates."

This is an internal tool, not a tagline. It tells designers who they are designing for and what must feel true.

### Personality with tensions

Personality becomes useful when it has **tensions** — pairs that define where the brand sits between two qualities. Use sliders:

| Scale | 1 ←→ 5 | Our position |
|---|---|---|
| Serious ←→ Playful | | 2 |
| Traditional ←→ Modern | | 4 |
| Exclusive ←→ Accessible | | 4 |
| Calm ←→ Energetic | | 3 |
| Refined ←→ Raw | | 2 |

"Serious but approachable, modern, refined" gives far clearer direction than "friendly and professional".

A second useful device is **"We are… but not…"**:

- We are confident, but not arrogant.
- We are expert, but not academic.
- We are warm, but not sugary.

These phrases stop designers and writers from overshooting a trait.

### Archetypes (use with care)

Some teams use brand archetypes (Hero, Sage, Explorer, Caregiver and so on) as shorthand. They can spark ideas, but they can also push brands toward clichés. Use them as a conversation starter, then write your own specific personality description.

### Verbal identity: voice and tone

- **Voice** is constant — the brand's personality in words.
- **Tone** flexes by context — more celebratory in a launch post, more careful in a complaint response.

A simple voice chart:

| Voice trait | Do | Don't |
|---|---|---|
| Clear | Short sentences, plain words | Jargon, buzzwords |
| Warm | Speak to "you", acknowledge feelings | Corporate passive voice |
| Confident | State benefits directly | Hype, exaggerated claims |

For bilingual brands, define voice for each language rather than translating word-for-word; humor, formality and honorifics work differently in Arabic, Urdu and English.

### Translating personality into visual cues

Designers can map traits to visual levers:

| Trait direction | Shape | Type | Color | Imagery |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Playful | Rounded, irregular | Rounded or quirky sans | Bright, varied | Candid, motion |
| Refined | Precise, thin lines | High-contrast serif or elegant sans | Restrained, deep | Composed, editorial |
| Energetic | Diagonals, dynamic | Bold, condensed | Warm, saturated | Action, close crops |
| Calm | Horizontal, open | Light to regular weights | Cool, muted | Space, soft light |
| Trustworthy | Stable, geometric | Sturdy, legible | Consistent, not garish | Real people, real places |

These are tendencies, not rules — context and execution matter — but they help you justify choices to clients with reasons instead of taste.

### Worked example: a finance creator

A Riyadh-based creator teaches young professionals to budget. Positioning: "practical money habits without guilt". Personality sliders: fairly serious about money (2), modern (4), very accessible (5), calm (2). "We are smart, but not preachy."

Visual direction: clean sans-serif with friendly proportions, a calm teal and warm sand palette, simple line icons, real photos of everyday life, generous whitespace. Voice: plain Arabic and English, encouraging, no shaming language, no promises of guaranteed returns (which could also raise regulatory issues for financial content).

### Common mistakes

- Generic adjectives shared by every competitor.
- Personality with no boundaries ("fun!") leading to off-brand extremes.
- Forcing an archetype that does not fit.
- Translating voice literally between languages.

### Hands-on: translate strategy into a design direction brief

```text
DESIGN DIRECTION BRIEF — [brand]
Positioning (one sentence): __________________________________
Personality sliders (1-5): Serious-Playful _ Traditional-Modern _
  Exclusive-Accessible _ Calm-Energetic _ Refined-Raw _
We are ___ but not ___  (×3)
Visual translation:
  Shape language:  geometric / organic / angular / rounded   → because ___
  Color direction: hue family, saturation, value            → because ___
  Type direction:  serif/sans/display, weight, width        → because ___
  Imagery:         candid/staged, light, casting            → because ___
  Motion:          quick/snappy vs slow/smooth              → because ___
Voice: 3 principles + example lines (headline, error message, DM reply)
Must avoid (category clichés): ___________________________
```

### Voice chart example

| Principle | Do | Don't |
|---|---|---|
| Clear, not clever | "Your order ships tomorrow." | "Good things come to those who wait 😉" |
| Warm, not sugary | "We've got you — here's how to fix it." | "OMG we're SO sorry babe 💕" |
| Expert, not academic | "Use SPF 30 daily, even indoors." | "Photoprotective efficacy is contingent upon…" |

For bilingual brands, write voice principles for each language rather than translating examples word for word — tone markers, formality and humor differ between English, Arabic and Urdu.

### Before/after: from adjectives to visual cues

| Strategy words | Weak translation | Strong translation |
|---|---|---|
| "Premium but approachable" | Black and gold, script font | Deep warm neutral + one rich accent, generous space, a humanist sans with a refined serif for headlines, candid (not glossy) photography |
| "Energetic, youthful" | Neon everything | One high-energy accent on a calm base, bold condensed type, dynamic diagonals, quick motion |

### Summary

Anchor identity work in a specific positioning statement, express personality through sliders and "we are… but not…" boundaries, define voice and tone, and map traits to visual levers so every design choice has a reason.

scenes.narration: Pick up any stack of design briefs and you'll see the same three words again and again. Modern. Trustworthy. Innovative. Every bank says it. Every clinic says it. Every startup says it. And that's the problem. Words that describe everyone guide no one. A designer can't make modern and trustworthy look different from the competitor who also asked for modern and trustworthy. In this lecture, you'll learn how to write a positioning statement that anchors decisions, how to define personality with tensions and sliders, how to create a verbal identity, and how to translate all of it into visual cues. By the end, you'll turn vague adjectives into a design direction someone can actually act on.

A brand that's a two on serious to playful, a four on traditional to modern, and a two on refined to raw is serious but approachable, modern and refined. Then add we are, but not statements. We are confident, but not arrogant. Expert, but not academic. Warm, but not sugary. These phrases stop designers and writers from overshooting. You can use archetypes too, but carefully, as a conversation starter, not a costume.

Tone adapts to the situation: you might be playful in a social post and calm in an apology. Write three voice principles, each with a do and a don't. Clear, not clever: your order ships tomorrow, not good things come to those who wait. Warm, not sugary. Expert, not academic. For bilingual brands, write principles for each language rather than translating examples word for word, because formality, humor and tone markers differ between English, Arabic and Urdu.

Type: a humanist sans with a large x-height, with numbers set bold. Imagery: candid photos of real, everyday spending moments, not piles of cash. Motion: quick and light. Shape language: geometric shapes feel precise and modern, organic shapes feel natural and human, angular shapes feel energetic or aggressive, rounded shapes feel friendly. lessons.title: Research, audits and the creative brief
lessons.body:
### Research prevents expensive guesswork

Identity decisions are hard to reverse once logos are on packaging, signs and thousands of posts. A short, focused research phase reduces risk and gives you evidence when presenting to clients.

### 1. Stakeholder and customer input

- **Stakeholder interviews:** founders, sales, customer service. Ask what the brand must never be, what customers praise and complain about, and where the business is going in the next few years.
- **Customer insight:** reviews, comments, DMs, support tickets and short interviews. Look for the words customers use — they often reveal what the brand really means to people.

### 2. Brand audit (for existing brands)

Collect every current touchpoint — logo files, social posts, website, packaging, invoices, signage, email signatures — into one board. Then assess:

```
Brand audit checklist
[ ] How many logo versions are in use? Are any outdated or distorted?
[ ] How many colors/fonts appear in practice vs. officially?
[ ] What do customers recognize us by? (ask them)
[ ] Which assets are distinctive and worth keeping?
[ ] Where is the identity failing (small sizes, dark mode, video, Arabic/Urdu script)?
[ ] What do we need that doesn't exist yet (templates, icon set, motion)?
```

An audit often reveals that the problem is not the logo but inconsistency — and that the brand already owns some valuable cues.

### 3. Competitive visual landscape

Gather competitors' logos, colors, websites and social feeds on one board. Look for **category conventions** — everyone in finance using blue, everyone in organic food using green and kraft paper, every fitness coach using black and neon.

Then decide deliberately:

- **Follow conventions** where they signal category membership and trust (people should instantly understand what you sell).
- **Break conventions** where you need to stand out — often color, typography or imagery style.

A common approach is to keep enough convention to be understood and break enough to be noticed.

### 4. Mood boards and visual territories

Rather than one mood board, create **two or three distinct territories** — different visual directions that all fit the strategy. For example, for a boutique travel agency:

- Territory A: "Modern heritage" — geometric patterns inspired by local architecture, deep jewel tones, elegant serif.
- Territory B: "Sunlit minimal" — light sand palette, lots of space, clean sans, airy photography.
- Territory C: "Bold explorer" — vivid color blocks, strong type, adventurous photography.

Present them with a sentence explaining how each expresses the strategy. The client chooses a direction before you spend time on logos. Be careful with mood-board images: they are references for discussion, not assets to copy.

### 5. The creative brief

Everything becomes a one- to two-page creative brief. A reusable template:

```
CREATIVE BRIEF — [Brand]
Background:           What's happening and why now?
Objective:            What must the identity achieve?
Audience:             Who, specifically? What do they value?
Positioning:          Our statement (one paragraph)
Personality:          Sliders + "we are… but not…"
Competitors:          Key players + category conventions
Keep / change:        Assets to protect; problems to fix
Deliverables:         Logo system, palette, type, icons, templates…
Applications:         Where it must work (social, app icon, signage…)
Languages/scripts:    e.g. English + Arabic
Constraints:          Budget, timeline, legal, existing materials
Success criteria:     How we will judge the result
Approvals:            Who signs off, and when
```

Get the brief **approved in writing** before design begins. When feedback later drifts ("can we try purple?"), you can refer back to agreed objectives.

### Worked example: a small agency's rebrand brief (excerpt)

- Objective: move from "cheap social media freelancers" perception to "performance creative partner for DTC brands".
- Keep: the name and the orange accent (clients recognize it).
- Change: clip-art style logo; inconsistent fonts; lack of case-study templates.
- Applications: LinkedIn, website, pitch decks, proposal documents, video intros.
- Success criteria: prospective clients describe the brand as "strategic" and "premium" in feedback sessions; the team can produce on-brand decks from templates without design help.

### Common mistakes

- Skipping research because "we know our brand".
- Presenting only one direction, turning the review into "like/dislike".
- Copying mood-board images into final work.
- Starting design without a signed-off brief.

### Hands-on: the creative brief template (identity projects)

```text
CREATIVE BRIEF — [brand] identity — v1 — date — owner
1. Background: business, stage, why now
2. Objective: what the identity must achieve (measurable where possible)
3. Audience: primary and secondary; markets and languages
4. Strategy summary: positioning, personality sliders, "we are… but not…"
5. Insights: customer language, audit findings, competitor conventions
6. Keep: distinctive assets with equity (color? symbol? name style?)
7. Deliverables: logo system, palette, type, imagery, icons, motion,
   templates, guidelines, asset library — formats and languages
8. Touchpoints: top 10 by importance (e.g. app icon, Instagram, packaging)
9. Constraints: budget, timeline, legal (trademark search), scripts,
   accessibility (WCAG 2.2 AA for digital), print methods
10. AI use: allowed for research/exploration? any restrictions? disclosure?
11. Decision makers and approval process
12. Success measures: recognition tests, consistency audit score, launch KPIs
```

### Research tools that speed things up (and their limits)

- **Boards:** Figma or FigJam, Miro, or a simple slide deck for the competitive landscape and audit.
- **Customer language:** export reviews, comments and survey answers; an AI assistant can cluster themes and pull representative quotes — verify every quote against the source, and anonymize personal data first.
- **Competitor scans:** screenshot competitors' social grids, websites and packaging on the same day; note colors, type styles, imagery and tone.
- **Moodboards:** AI image tools can help visualize visual territories quickly; label AI-generated boards as exploratory, and never present them as final work or reuse them as assets without rights checks.

### Before/after: a brief that prevents rework

| Missing in the "before" brief | Consequence | Added in the "after" brief |
|---|---|---|
| Arabic lockup | Logo redesigned late when Arabic version didn't fit | Scripts: English + Arabic, both first-class |
| Keep list | Designer replaced the orange customers recognized | Keep: signature orange and rounded shape language |
| Decision makers | CEO saw the work for the first time at final presentation | CEO joins the direction-approval meeting |
| Accessibility | Brand teal failed as text color on the website | WCAG 2.2 AA for digital pairings |

### Summary

Gather stakeholder and customer insight, audit existing touchpoints, map category conventions, explore two or three territories, and capture decisions in an approved creative brief.

scenes.narration: Imagine spending six weeks designing a beautiful new identity for a client. You present it. The CEO, who you've never met, says, where's our orange? Customers know us by the orange. And by the way, where's the Arabic version? Six weeks, and you've designed the wrong thing. That story is painfully common, and it's almost always a research and brief problem, not a design problem. In this lecture, you'll learn how to gather stakeholder and customer input, run a brand audit, map the competitive landscape, build moodboards and visual territories, and write a creative brief that prevents rework. By the end, you'll start every identity project with evidence instead of guesswork.

lessons.title: Logo types and the principles of a great logo
lessons.body:
### What a logo is for

A logo is a signature: a compact mark that identifies the brand and, over time, accumulates meaning. It does not need to explain everything the company does. Many strong logos are simple and say little literally; their meaning comes from consistent use alongside good products and experiences.

### Types of logo

| Type | Description | Strengths | Watch-outs |
|---|---|---|---|
| Wordmark (logotype) | The name set in distinctive type | Builds name recognition; good for new brands | Long names can be hard at small sizes |
| Lettermark (monogram) | Initials | Compact; good for long names | Initials alone carry little meaning at first |
| Pictorial mark | A recognizable image or icon | Memorable; works as app icon | Can be too literal or generic |
| Abstract mark | A non-literal shape | Ownable, flexible | Needs time and consistency to gain meaning |
| Mascot / character | An illustrated character | Friendly, great for content | Can be complex to reproduce small |
| Emblem | Text inside a badge or crest | Heritage, authority | Detail often lost at small sizes |
| Combination mark | Symbol plus wordmark | Flexible: use together or apart | Needs clear lockup rules |

Most small brands benefit from a **combination system**: a wordmark for recognition plus a simple symbol or monogram for small spaces such as profile pictures, favicons and app icons.

### Principles of an effective logo

1. **Simple** — few elements, easy to recognize and recall.
2. **Distinctive** — does not look like competitors or common stock icons (lightbulbs for ideas, globes for "international", generic swooshes).
3. **Scalable** — works from a 16 px favicon to a large sign.
4. **Versatile** — works in one color, reversed on dark backgrounds, on photos, embroidered or engraved.
5. **Appropriate** — fits the personality and audience.
6. **Durable** — avoids short-lived trends that will date quickly.

A useful test: **could someone sketch it from memory after seeing it a few times?**

### Multi-script logos

Brands operating in Arabic- and English-speaking markets often need bilingual logos. Good practice:

- Design both scripts together so they share weight, rhythm and visual height, rather than pairing an existing Latin logo with an off-the-shelf Arabic font.
- Work with designers or type specialists who read the script fluently; letter joins and proportions matter.
- Define lockups for Arabic-first and English-first contexts, and single-script versions.

### Testing a logo concept

```
Logo evaluation scorecard (1–5 each)
Simplicity          __
Distinctiveness     __ (compared against competitor board)
Small-size clarity  __ (16 px, 32 px, profile circle)
One-color / reversed __
Appropriateness     __ (vs. personality sliders)
Memorability        __ (sketch-from-memory test)
Legal risk check    __ (preliminary search done?)
```

### Worked example: logo for a Karachi-based tech tutoring startup

Name: "Qadam" (meaning "step"). Personality: encouraging, modern, accessible.

- Concept 1 (rejected): a graduation cap with a lightbulb — generic and literal; many education brands use it.
- Concept 2 (rejected): an intricate emblem with a circuit pattern — fails at small sizes.
- Concept 3 (chosen): a custom wordmark in Latin and Urdu scripts sharing a rounded, friendly stroke, plus a simple symbol made of three ascending steps that also suggests a "Q". Works as an app icon, prints in one color, and gives meaning ("step by step") without being literal.

### Common mistakes

- Trying to show everything the business does in one mark.
- Relying on trendy effects (gradients, 3D, thin lines) that fail in one color or at small size.
- Using stock icons or templates — they are not distinctive, and may not be registrable as trademarks.
- Evaluating logos only at large size on a white background.

### Presenting logo types to clients

Clients often arrive with a fixed idea ("we need an icon like the big tech brands"). Walk them through the trade-offs using their own situation: how well known the name is, where the logo will appear most, whether the name is long, and whether they need an app icon or profile image. A new business with an unfamiliar name usually gains more from a strong wordmark than from an abstract symbol that nobody yet associates with them. Show two or three types applied to the same real touchpoints so the decision is based on use, not on logos seen in isolation.

### Responsive logos: one identity, several sizes

Modern identities plan how the logo **simplifies as it shrinks** — often called a responsive logo system.

| Size tier | Typical use | What's shown |
|---|---|---|
| Large | Signage, website hero, packaging front | Full combination mark with tagline (if any) |
| Medium | Website header, email signature, documents | Symbol + wordmark, no tagline |
| Small | Social profile picture, watermark | Symbol or monogram only |
| Tiny | Favicon, app icon, notification badge | Simplified symbol with thicker strokes and fewer details |

### Hands-on: logo evaluation scorecard

Score each concept 1–5; anything scoring 1–2 on distinctiveness or small-size legibility needs rework before presenting.

```text
LOGO SCORECARD — concept: __________
Simple (few elements, easy to recall)                 1 2 3 4 5
Distinctive (vs competitor board and stock icons)     1 2 3 4 5
Appropriate (fits positioning and personality)        1 2 3 4 5
Legible at 16 px and in a circle crop                 1 2 3 4 5
Works in one color (black; white on dark)             1 2 3 4 5
Scalable (embroidery, signage, app icon)              1 2 3 4 5
Script-ready (Arabic/Urdu/other lockups if needed)    1 2 3 4 5
No unintended meanings in target languages/markets    pass / fail
Total: ___/35   Notes: ___________________________
```

### Before/after: a tutoring startup's mark

| Test | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| 16 px favicon | Detailed lightbulb with a graduation cap — unrecognizable blob | Bold "Q" monogram with a step-shaped counter — clear |
| Distinctiveness | Three competitors use lightbulbs | Unique letter-based symbol |
| One color | Relied on a gradient | Solid shapes, works in black or white |
| Urdu lockup | Not considered | Wordmark set in both scripts with matched weight |

### Summary

Choose the logo type that fits the name and use cases — often a combination system — and judge concepts on simplicity, distinctiveness, scalability, versatility, appropriateness and durability.

lessons.title: The logo design process: from sketch to vector
lessons.body:
### Process beats inspiration

Professional logo design is not a single flash of genius. It is a structured process of generating many ideas, filtering them against the brief, and refining the best ones with craft. A clear process also makes client conversations easier, because every step has a reason.

### Step 1: Word and concept mapping

Start with language, not visuals. From the brief, list:

- Keywords about the business, audience and personality.
- Associations, metaphors and stories (for "Qadam" = step: progress, path, stairs, footprint, rhythm).
- Cultural references that are relevant and respectful for the markets served.
- Clichés to avoid (the first ideas everyone would have).

Pick several promising **concept routes** — for example "steps and progress", "the letter Q", "a path".

### Step 2: Rapid sketching

Sketch quickly on paper or a tablet — dozens of small thumbnails, no detail. Quantity matters here: early ideas are often obvious; better ideas appear after the obvious ones are out of the way. Work each concept route and also explore the name's letterforms.

### Step 3: Select and digitize

Choose a handful of the strongest sketches that fit the brief. Build them as **vectors** in a vector tool, paying attention to:

- **Geometry and optical correction** — shapes that are mathematically equal can look unequal. Circles often need to be slightly larger than squares to look the same size; horizontal strokes often need to be slightly thinner than vertical ones to look equal.
- **Consistent stroke weights and corner radii.**
- **Negative space** — the spaces inside and around the mark are part of the design.

### Step 4: Typography for the wordmark

- Start from a suitable typeface **with a license that permits logo use**, or draw custom lettering.
- Customize: adjust kerning carefully, modify distinctive letters, align weights with the symbol.
- Custom or modified lettering increases distinctiveness and reduces the risk of looking like a template.

### Step 5: Stress-test

Before presenting, test each concept:

```
Stress tests
[ ] 16 px favicon and 32 px app/profile sizes
[ ] Circle crop (social profile pictures)
[ ] One color: black, white on dark
[ ] On a busy photo
[ ] Embroidery / engraving (no hairlines, limited detail)
[ ] Next to competitor logos
[ ] Upside-down / rotated (reveals unwanted shapes)
[ ] Check for unintended meanings or shapes in all target languages
```

The last test matters: marks can accidentally resemble offensive symbols, rude shapes or other brands. Ask people from each target market to review.

### Step 6: Present in context

Clients judge logos better when they see them in use. For each concept, show:

- The concept rationale (one or two sentences tied to the brief).
- The mark in black and white first — a good logo should work without color.
- Mock-ups: app icon, social profile, website header, business card or packaging, signage.

Present two or three strong concepts at most; ten options overwhelm and signal a lack of conviction.

### Step 7: Refine

After selection, refine: tweak proportions, finalize the wordmark, align symbol and text, and prepare variations (covered in the next lesson). Keep revision rounds defined in your contract to avoid endless iterations.

### A note on AI tools in logo work

AI tools can help with early exploration: generating mood references, testing a concept route quickly, or producing vector sketches (some tools, such as Recraft and Adobe Illustrator's generative features, output editable vectors). But using a generated image directly as a logo is risky:

- **Similarity:** outputs can resemble existing marks — run visual and trademark searches.
- **Protection:** the US Copyright Office's January 2025 report concluded that prompts alone do not make someone the author of an output; protection depends on sufficient human expressive contribution. A human-designed, human-refined mark is far easier to protect and to assign to a client.
- **Craft:** generated marks are often hard to edit into clean, optically corrected vectors and rarely pass the small-size tests.

Professional practice: AI for exploration (label it as such in presentations), humans for the final mark, and a written record of the human design process. Check local law and each tool's terms.

### Worked example: a halal skincare brand

Concept routes: "purity and water", "the initial letter", "botanical growth". After sketching many thumbnails, three were digitized: a droplet formed by two leaves, a monogram with a crescent-like negative space, and a clean custom wordmark. The droplet-leaf was too similar to several competitors on the board, so it was dropped. The monogram failed the 16 px test until the negative space was widened. Final presentation: the refined monogram system and the wordmark, each shown on packaging, a phone screen and a shop label.

### Common mistakes

- Starting on the computer and skipping sketching.
- Presenting logos only on white artboards.
- Ignoring font licenses for logo use.
- Skipping unintended-meaning and competitor-similarity checks.

### Hands-on: build a mark in Figma (or Illustrator)

1. **Set up** a frame at 1000 × 1000 with a 10 × 10 layout grid and a circle guide for profile crops.
2. **Block out** the symbol with basic shapes (rectangle, ellipse, polygon). Keep them editable.
3. **Combine** shapes with boolean operations (Union, Subtract, Intersect, Exclude) to create the silhouette; flatten only when final.
4. **Refine curves** with the pen tool / vector edit mode: fewer anchor points, smooth handles, consistent corner radii.
5. **Optical corrections:** make round shapes slightly overshoot the baseline and cap height; thin horizontal strokes slightly; widen tight counters so they survive at 16 px.
6. **Wordmark:** outline the licensed typeface, then adjust kerning and customize one or two letters.
7. **Test** inside the same file: duplicate the mark at 16, 32 and 64 px, in a circle, in black and white, and next to competitor logos.
8. **Export** SVG for review and a PDF for print checks.

### Hands-on: present in context with mockups

- Show every concept on the same set of mockups: app icon, social profile (circle), website header, business card or packaging, signage, and a dark-mode UI.
- Use **smart objects** in Photoshop mockup templates, or frames with image fills in Figma, so one replaced file updates every mockup.
- Check mockup licenses (many are free for personal use only) and don't imply real placements (for example a billboard) that aren't planned.
- If you use AI-generated scenes as mockup backgrounds, label them as visualizations.

```text
CONCEPT PRESENTATION SLIDE (per concept)
Title: Concept name + one-line idea
Rationale: 2 sentences tied to the brief (positioning, personality)
Black & white mark → color mark → 16 px / circle crop
Mockups: app icon · social profile · website header · packaging · signage
What it enables: pattern, icon style, motion idea
```

### Summary

Map concepts in words, sketch widely, digitize the best with optical care, stress-test at small sizes and in context, present a few rationale-backed options, and refine within agreed revision rounds.

But behind it there's almost always a process: dozens of ideas, most of them thrown away, careful refinement, and a lot of testing. Process is what makes good logos repeatable, and what makes client conversations calm, because every step has a reason. In this lecture, you'll learn the seven steps of logo design, from concept mapping to refinement, how to build a mark in Figma, how to present concepts in mockups, and how to use AI tools responsibly. By the end, you'll have a process you can run on any logo project.

lessons.title: Logo systems, usage rules and protection
lessons.body:
### One logo, many situations

A single logo file is not enough. Brands appear in square profile pictures, horizontal website headers, vertical signs, tiny favicons, embroidered uniforms and video end cards. A **logo system** provides the right version for each situation and rules that keep it consistent.

### Core variations

| Variation | Use |
|---|---|
| Primary lockup | Default version when space allows |
| Horizontal lockup | Website headers, email signatures, banners |
| Stacked lockup | Square or vertical spaces |
| Symbol / monogram only | Profile pictures, app icons, favicons, social watermarks |
| Wordmark only | When the symbol is already present or too small |
| Bilingual lockups | Script-first versions for different markets |

### Color versions

- **Full color** on light backgrounds.
- **Reversed** (white or light) on dark or brand-color backgrounds.
- **One color black** and **one color white** for single-color printing, engraving, embossing and partner materials.
- Optional: a version for photographic backgrounds.

### Usage rules

**Clear space:** define a minimum empty area around the logo, often measured using a part of the logo itself (for example the height of a letter), so it scales with the logo.

**Minimum size:** the smallest size at which the logo remains legible — define it in pixels for screens and millimeters for print, and specify which variation to use below it (for example the symbol only).

**Placement:** preferred corners or positions for social templates, video watermarks and documents.

**Misuse examples** ("don'ts"):

```
Don't:
- Stretch or squash the logo
- Change the colors outside approved versions
- Add shadows, outlines or effects
- Rotate or rearrange elements
- Place on busy backgrounds without the approved treatment
- Recreate the wordmark by typing it in a font
- Put the logo inside another shape not in the guidelines
```

### File delivery

Deliver a logo pack that covers print and digital:

```
/Logo
  /Primary    SVG, PDF (vector), PNG (transparent, several sizes)
  /Horizontal SVG, PDF, PNG
  /Stacked    SVG, PDF, PNG
  /Symbol     SVG, PDF, PNG, app-icon and favicon sizes
  /Mono       black and white versions
  /Print      CMYK PDF, spot color versions if used
README        which file to use where
```

Name files predictably: brand_logo_horizontal_fullcolor_rgb.svg.

### Protecting the logo: trademark basics

This is general information, not legal advice; trademark law is territorial and varies by country.

- **Search before you commit.** Check official trademark databases in the countries where the brand operates (for example national IP offices in the UK, US, Pakistan, the UAE and Saudi Arabia, plus the WIPO Global Brand Database) and search the market for similar names and marks in the same category.
- **Distinctiveness matters.** Descriptive names and generic symbols are harder to protect.
- **Registration is by class and territory.** Trademarks are registered for specific goods/services classes and countries. International routes such as the Madrid System can simplify filing in multiple countries.
- **Ownership of design work.** In many jurisdictions, a freelancer owns copyright in their design until it is assigned in writing. Contracts should clearly transfer rights in the final logo to the client on payment, and state which fonts or third-party elements need separate licenses.
- **Use a professional.** For important brands, involve a trademark attorney or agent.

### Worked example: a creator's logo system

A YouTube and Instagram creator, "Noor Makes", commissions an identity:

- Primary: custom wordmark "Noor Makes" with a small star-shaped symbol.
- Symbol only: the star inside a circle for profile pictures and watermark.
- Horizontal: for YouTube channel art and website header.
- Color versions: deep purple on cream; cream on purple; black; white.
- Clear space: height of the "N" on all sides. Minimum width: 120 px for the wordmark; below that, the symbol only.
- Watermark rule: symbol at 60% opacity, bottom-right safe area on videos.
- Contract: copyright in the final logo assigned to the creator on final payment; font license purchased in the creator's name.

### Common mistakes

- Delivering one PNG and nothing else.
- No minimum size or small-size alternative.
- Skipping trademark searches until after launch.
- Assuming the client owns the design without a written assignment.

### Hands-on: logo export specs for digital touchpoints

| Asset | Format | Size / notes |
|---|---|---|
| Master files | SVG + PDF (vector) | Outlined text; RGB for screen, CMYK/spot versions for print |
| Website favicon | SVG favicon plus ICO/PNG fallback | Include 16, 32 and 48 px renderings of the simplified symbol |
| Apple touch icon | PNG | 180 × 180 px |
| App store icon | PNG | 1024 × 1024 px for Apple's App Store (check each store's current specs) |
| Social profile picture | PNG | Square, at least 400 × 400 px; keep the symbol inside the circle crop |
| Video watermark | PNG with transparency | Symbol only; define opacity and position |
| Email signature | PNG | Horizontal lockup at 2× for sharpness; keep file small |

### Trademark checklist (general information, not legal advice)

```text
[ ] Knockout search: official databases in each market — e.g. USPTO (US),
    UKIPO (UK), EUIPO (EU), IPO Pakistan, SAIP (Saudi Arabia), the UAE's
    trademark office, plus WIPO's Global Brand Database
[ ] Search the market: app stores, social handles, domains, marketplaces
[ ] Identify goods/services classes (Nice Classification)
[ ] Decide route: national filings or the Madrid System for several countries
[ ] Written assignment of copyright in the final logo to the client
[ ] Font and third-party element licenses cover logo use
[ ] Calendar: renewals, and monitoring for copycats
[ ] Trademark attorney/agent involved for important brands
```

### Before/after: a delivery that works

| | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Files | One PNG with a white background | SVG/PDF masters, PNGs per lockup, favicon and app icon set, mono versions |
| Guidance | None | One-page logo usage sheet: variations, clear space, minimum sizes, don'ts |
| Rights | "It's yours" in a DM | Signed assignment on final payment; font license in the client's name |
| Protection | Name used for a year before searching | Searches before launch; filing in key markets |

### Summary

Build a logo system with lockups, a symbol, color versions, clear space and minimum sizes, deliver an organized file pack, and handle trademark searches and rights transfer properly.

In this lecture, you'll learn how to build a logo system with variations and color versions, write usage rules, deliver a proper file pack with export specs, and handle trademark and ownership basics. By the end, your logos will work in every situation, and they'll be protected.

lessons.title: Brand color systems and design tokens
lessons.body:
### From favorite colors to a system

A brand palette is not a mood board of pleasant colors. It is a working system that must deliver recognition, hierarchy and accessibility across screens, print, merchandise and partner materials — and be easy for others to apply correctly.

### Structure of a brand color system

| Role | Purpose | Typical count |
|---|---|---|
| Primary (signature) | The recognizable brand color | 1 (sometimes 2) |
| Secondary | Supports variety in layouts, campaigns, illustrations | 2–4 |
| Accent | Calls to action, highlights | 1 |
| Neutrals | Text, backgrounds, borders | 3–6 |
| Functional | Success, warning, error, info (for digital products) | 3–4 |

The **signature color** should be used consistently and prominently enough to become associated with the brand. Secondary colors add range but should not overpower it.

### Choosing the signature color

Consider:

1. **Differentiation** — how does it compare with competitors' colors (from your landscape board)?
2. **Personality fit** — does its hue, saturation and value express the personality sliders?
3. **Practicality** — can it be reproduced consistently on screens, in print, on fabric and signage? Very vivid screen colors may be impossible to match in CMYK.
4. **Accessibility** — can it carry text, or will it need a darker/lighter variant?
5. **Cultural context** — are there strong associations in your key markets that help or hinder?

### Specifying colors for every medium

Each color should be defined in all the systems it will be used in:

```
Color: Signature Teal
HEX     #0F766E
RGB     15 118 110
CMYK    per printer proof (conversion is not exact — proof it)
Spot    Pantone/other spot reference if used for print
Usage   Headlines on light bg, key shapes, app icon background
Text    White text passes AA on this color at normal sizes? verify
```

Always check CMYK and spot matches with physical proofs; automatic conversions can be noticeably off, especially for bright blues, greens and oranges.

### Tints, shades and ramps

Create a ramp for each main color — for example 50 to 900 — so designers have lighter backgrounds and darker text versions that are still "on brand". Many digital teams generate ramps with perceptual color tools so steps look evenly spaced. Mark which steps are approved for text on white and on dark backgrounds.

### Accessibility built in

Include an **approved pairings matrix** in the system:

| Text / Background | White | Sand-50 | Teal-700 | Navy-900 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Navy-900 | ✓ AA | ✓ AA | ✗ | — |
| White | — | ✗ | ✓ AA | ✓ AA |
| Teal-700 | ✓ AA | ✓ AA | — | ✗ |

(Verify each pairing with a contrast checker; the table above is an illustration of the format.) Designers then choose from approved pairs rather than testing each time.

### Design tokens

Design tokens are named, platform-agnostic values for design decisions — colors, type sizes, spacing, radii — used consistently across design tools and code. A simple structure:

```
Primitive tokens          Semantic tokens
teal-700 = #0F766E   →    color.brand.primary = teal-700
navy-900 = #0B1B34   →    color.text.default   = navy-900
sand-50  = #FBF7F0   →    color.bg.canvas      = sand-50
coral-500 = #F26B4F  →    color.action.primary = coral-500
```

Semantic names ("text default", "action primary") make it easy to update the system later, support dark mode, and help developers and designers speak the same language. Tools such as Figma support variables that map to tokens, and many code frameworks consume token files.

### Dark mode and backgrounds

Plan how the palette behaves on dark backgrounds — for apps, video end cards and dark-mode social feeds. Dark mode is not a simple inversion: saturated colors can vibrate on dark backgrounds and may need adjusted variants.

### Worked example: palette for a Dubai-based property content creator

- Signature: deep emerald (differentiates from competitors' gold and black).
- Secondary: warm sand and soft stone for backgrounds; a muted sky blue for charts.
- Accent: a brass-gold used only for calls to action and key figures.
- Neutrals: ink, charcoal, mid-gray, off-white.
- Tokens: color.brand.primary, color.action.primary, color.bg.canvas, color.text.muted.
- Pairings matrix: white on emerald ✓; brass on off-white ✗ for text (used only for shapes and buttons with ink text).

### Common mistakes

- Too many "primary" colors competing.
- Only specifying HEX, causing inconsistent print and merchandise.
- No accessible text pairings, leading to low-contrast designs.
- Naming tokens by appearance only ("light-blue-2"), making future changes painful.

### Hands-on: brand color tokens from Figma to code

1. In Figma, create a **Primitives** collection (`teal/50…900`, `navy/900`, `sand/50`, `coral/500`) and a **Semantic** collection with Light and Dark modes (`color/text/default`, `color/bg/canvas`, `color/action/primary`…) that reference primitives.
2. Apply only semantic variables in designs and templates.
3. Export or sync tokens for developers. Many teams use a JSON format based on the W3C Design Tokens Community Group specification (check the group's site for its current status), via a plugin or Figma's variables features/API, then transform it for CSS, iOS and Android with a tool such as Style Dictionary.

```json
{
  "color": {
    "teal": {
      "700": { "$type": "color", "$value": "#0F766E" }
    },
    "text": {
      "default": { "$type": "color", "$value": "{color.navy.900}" }
    },
    "action": {
      "primary": { "$type": "color", "$value": "{color.coral.500}" }
    }
  }
}
```

```css
:root {
  --color-teal-700: #0F766E;
  --color-text-default: #0B1B34;
  --color-action-primary: #F26B4F;
}
@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) {
  :root { --color-text-default: #F5F2EC; }
}
```

(Hex values are this lesson's illustrative palette.)

### Brand color spec template

```text
COLOR: Signature Teal (primary)
HEX #0F766E · RGB 15 118 110 · CMYK: from printer proof · Spot: if used
Token: color.brand.primary → teal-700
Approved text pairings: white on teal-700 (verify ≥ 4.5:1); teal-700 on sand-50
Not for: small text on navy; large fills in print without a proof
Share of use: ~30% of a typical layout (signature, not wallpaper)
```

### Before/after: a Dubai property creator's palette

| | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Colors | Gold, black, white — like every luxury competitor | Warm sand base, deep teal signature, restrained brass accent |
| Accessibility | Gold text on white failed contrast | Pairings matrix; gold/brass used only for large graphics or on dark |
| Print | Screen gold printed muddy | Spot/metallic spec for print, proofed physically |
| Digital | Hex values typed by hand | Semantic tokens with light and dark modes |

### Summary

Structure the palette by role, specify each color for every medium with physical proofs, build ramps, publish approved accessible pairings, and express decisions as semantic design tokens.

lessons.title: Brand typography systems
lessons.body:
### Typography is a brand asset

Typefaces can be as recognizable as colors or logos. Consistent brand typography makes every post, slide and web page feel like it comes from the same place — even without a logo.

### Anatomy of a brand type system

| Component | Decision |
|---|---|
| Primary typeface | Headlines and brand expression |
| Secondary typeface | Body text, UI, long reading |
| Scripts | Arabic, Urdu or other scripts and their pairings |
| Weights and styles | Which weights are allowed (e.g. Regular, Semibold, Bold) |
| Type scale | Named sizes for digital and print |
| Rules | Case, tracking, leading, alignment, emphasis |
| Fallbacks | System fonts when brand fonts are unavailable (email, some documents) |

### Choosing brand typefaces

Beyond the fundamentals (legibility, tone, pairing), brand typography needs:

- **Distinctiveness:** very common default fonts make a brand look generic. A distinctive headline face — or a customized one — helps recognition.
- **Range:** enough weights to create hierarchy across many applications.
- **Language support:** all needed scripts and characters, designed to work together.
- **Licensing for every use:** desktop (design team), web embedding, app embedding, broadcast/video, logo, and number of users. Commercial licenses differ — budget for them.
- **Availability for partners and staff:** if non-designers create documents, consider how they will access fonts (shared brand kits in online tools, open-license families, or approved fallbacks).

### Custom and bespoke type

Larger brands sometimes commission a custom typeface, which increases distinctiveness and can simplify licensing. For small brands, a sensible middle route is a carefully chosen licensed family plus a **custom wordmark** in the logo.

### Multi-script systems

For brands in Pakistan, the Gulf and beyond:

- Choose Latin and Arabic-script faces with compatible weight, contrast and visual size. Some type families are designed in both scripts together.
- Remember Arabic script is typically set with different vertical proportions; don't force identical cap heights.
- Nastaliq (common for Urdu) has distinctive diagonal flow and needs extra line height.
- Define rules for bilingual layouts: which language leads, alignment (right for Arabic/Urdu, left for English), and how to mirror layouts.
- Have native readers review typography — awkward joins or wrong letterforms damage credibility.

### Type scale and rules

Define a named scale that works for both digital and print, for example:

```
Brand type scale (digital, base 16 px)
display   56 / 60 line-height, Bold, tracking −1%
h1        40 / 48, Bold
h2        32 / 40, Semibold
h3        24 / 32, Semibold
body      16 / 24, Regular
small     14 / 20, Regular
label     12 / 16, Semibold, uppercase, tracking +4%
```

Add social-specific sizes (larger) because canvases are scaled down on phones.

Rules to document:

- Headline case: sentence case or title case? (Sentence case often feels more modern and friendly.)
- When uppercase is allowed (labels, short tags).
- Alignment defaults.
- Emphasis method (weight or color, not both).
- Numerals: lining or old-style; tabular for tables.

### Fallback fonts

Email clients, some office documents and certain platforms cannot use custom fonts. Specify fallbacks (for example a widely available system sans-serif) with similar proportions so layouts do not break and the brand still looks tidy.

### Worked example: type system for a professional-services firm in Riyadh

- Primary: a contemporary serif for English headlines (authority, editorial feel), paired with a modern Arabic typeface with similar contrast.
- Secondary: a humanist sans in Latin and a matching Arabic sans for body and UI.
- Weights: Regular, Medium, Bold only.
- Rules: sentence case headlines in English; right-aligned Arabic; bilingual documents lead with Arabic on official materials.
- Fallbacks: system sans in email; an open-license serif in office templates.
- Licenses: desktop for five designers, web for the website, app embedding for the client portal.

### Common mistakes

- Choosing a font the brand cannot legally use in apps or video.
- Specifying only English typography for a bilingual brand.
- Allowing every weight in a large family, which reduces consistency.
- No fallbacks, causing broken emails and documents.

### Hands-on: licensing matrix and fallback stacks

Before you finalize a type system, confirm the license covers every use.

| Use | Needed? | License type to check | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Design team desktop | Yes | Desktop, number of users | Freelancers may need their own seats |
| Website | Yes | Web font (often by page views) | Or self-host an open-license family |
| Mobile app | Maybe | App embedding | Often separate from web |
| Logo / wordmark | Yes | Logo use permitted? | Some licenses restrict or require extra terms |
| Video / broadcast / ads | Maybe | Broadcast or digital ads | Check for paid campaigns |
| Partners and staff documents | Maybe | Open-license family or approved fallback | Non-designers need access |

Fallback stacks keep layouts tidy where brand fonts can't load (email, some office tools):

```css
/* Headline: brand serif, then similar widely available fonts */
--font-headline: "Brand Serif", Georgia, "Times New Roman", serif;
/* Body: brand sans, then system UI fonts */
--font-body: "Brand Sans", system-ui, -apple-system, "Segoe UI", Roboto, Arial, sans-serif;
/* Arabic / Urdu body with explicit fallbacks */
--font-arabic: "Brand Arabic", "Noto Naskh Arabic", "Segoe UI", Tahoma, sans-serif;
```

### Brand type style sheet (template)

```text
PRIMARY (headlines): [family] — weights allowed: Bold, Semibold
SECONDARY (body/UI):  [family] — Regular, Medium, Semibold
SCRIPTS:              Arabic [family] (Naskh style); Urdu [family] (Nastaliq for social, Naskh for UI)
SCALE (digital):      display 56/60 · h1 40/48 · h2 32/40 · body 16/24 · small 14/20 · label 12/16
SCALE (social 1080):  display 96 · h1 64 · h2 44 · body 32 · caption 24
RULES: sentence case headlines · one emphasis method · left-align (English), right-align (Arabic/Urdu)
       tabular numerals in tables · line height +20% for Nastaliq
FALLBACKS: see stacks above
LICENSES:  desktop ✓ web ✓ app ✗ (not needed yet) logo ✓ — owner: [name], renewal: [date]
```

### Before/after: a Riyadh professional-services firm

| | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Families | Five fonts across decks, website and reports | One Latin serif + one bilingual sans with Arabic companion |
| Arabic | Default system font, mismatched weights | Designed companion with matched color and rhythm |
| Licensing | Web font used without a web license | Licensing matrix completed; web and app licenses purchased |
| Documents | Broke when fonts were missing | Fallback stack specified in templates |

### Summary

Treat typography as a brand asset: choose distinctive, legible, well-licensed families that cover all scripts, define a named scale and clear rules, and specify fallbacks for environments where brand fonts cannot load.

By the end, you'll build a type system that works everywhere.

lessons.title: Imagery, icons, patterns and motion
lessons.body:
### The supporting cast

Logo, color and type are the core, but most of what audiences actually see is **imagery, graphic elements and motion**. A brand with a consistent supporting system is recognizable even when the logo is absent — which on social media is most of the time.

### Photography style

Define a photography style that expresses the personality:

| Dimension | Options |
|---|---|
| Subject | People, product, places, process, results |
| Casting | Diverse, authentic, representative of the real audience |
| Framing | Close-up, environmental, flat-lay |
| Light | Natural and soft, high-contrast, studio |
| Color treatment | Warm, cool, desaturated, brand-tinted |
| Mood | Candid and energetic, calm and composed |
| Avoid | Clichés, obvious stock poses, over-retouching |

Include **do and don't examples** in guidelines. Specify consent and model-release requirements for people, and respect local norms — for example, modest dress and appropriate settings for campaigns in conservative markets, and permissions when photographing in public or religious spaces.

### Illustration style

If you use illustrations, specify line weight, color use, level of detail, how people are depicted and whether shading or texture is used. Mixing illustration styles from different sources is one of the fastest ways to make a brand feel inconsistent.

### Iconography

A consistent icon set needs:

- One style (outline or filled; sometimes duotone).
- Consistent stroke weight, corner radius and grid (for example a 24 px grid with 2 px strokes).
- Consistent metaphors (the same icon always means the same thing).
- Accessibility: icons that convey meaning need text labels or accessible names in digital products.

It is often efficient to start from a well-made, properly licensed icon library and customize it to match the brand.

### Graphic devices and patterns

Many memorable identities rely on a **graphic device** — a shape, frame, line, crop or pattern derived from the logo or strategy. Examples:

- A corner shape from the logo used to frame photos.
- A pattern inspired by local architecture or textiles (researched respectfully, not appropriated from specific sacred or protected designs).
- A highlight underline used on key words in headlines.
- A consistent way of cropping photos into a signature shape.

Graphic devices are powerful distinctive assets because they appear in every post, slide and package.

### Data visualization

For brands that publish charts, define chart colors, label style, gridline weight and a rule for highlighting key data. This prevents rainbow charts and keeps reports on-brand.

### Motion and sonic identity

Video and short-form content make motion essential:

- **Logo animation**: a short sting (often a second or two) for intros and end cards.
- **Motion principles**: speed (snappy or gentle), easing, how elements enter and exit.
- **Transitions and text animation**: consistent styles for captions and titles.
- **Sonic cues**: a short audio mnemonic, consistent music style, or a voice style. If you use AI-generated voices or music, check licenses and ensure voice cloning uses a real person's voice only with their consent.

Keep motion accessible: avoid rapid flashing and respect reduced-motion settings in digital products.

### Worked example: supporting system for a fitness studio in London

- Photography: real members (with consent), natural light, mid-workout energy, warm treatment, no heavily retouched bodies.
- Graphic device: a diagonal "pulse" line from the logo used to divide layouts and underline key words.
- Icons: filled style, rounded corners, matching the logo's radius.
- Motion: fast, punchy entries with a slight overshoot; logo sting under two seconds; captions in brand sans with a highlight bar.
- Sound: a short percussive sting, licensed for commercial use.

### Supporting-system checklist

```
[ ] Photography style with do/don't examples and consent rules
[ ] Illustration style (if used)
[ ] Icon style specs and library
[ ] Graphic device(s) and pattern rules
[ ] Chart/data style
[ ] Motion principles, logo animation, caption style
[ ] Sonic cues and licenses
```

### Common mistakes

- Relying on the logo alone for recognition.
- Mixing icon and illustration styles.
- Generic stock photography unrelated to real customers.
- Motion with no rules, creating inconsistent video content.

### AI imagery inside a brand system (2026)

Many brands now use AI image tools for backgrounds, illustrations and variations. Treat AI style as part of the supporting system:

- Document an **AI style kit**: written style spec, approved style references, prompt snippets, allowed uses (for example backgrounds and spot illustrations) and banned uses (real customers, product results, news-like scenes). See the AI Image Generation and Design course for the full workflow.
- Keep products real (photograph and composite them), and never generate real people without consent.
- Keep provenance data (Content Credentials) and follow platform labels for realistic AI content.

### Hands-on: an icon spec and motion principles

```text
ICON SPEC
Grid: 24 × 24 px, 2 px padding (live area 20 × 20)
Stroke: 2 px, round caps and joins; corner radius 2 px
Style: outline (filled variant only for selected/active states)
Metaphors: one meaning per icon (e.g. "bookmark" always = save)
Export: SVG, currentColor fills so icons inherit text color
Accessibility: every meaningful icon has a visible label or accessible name

MOTION PRINCIPLES
Personality: calm and confident → ease-out, 200-300 ms for UI, 0.8-1.5 s for logo stings
Entrances: fade + 8 px rise; exits: fade only
Logo sting: ≤ 2 s, ends on the static primary lockup
Accessibility: no flashing; respect reduced-motion settings (CSS prefers-reduced-motion)
```

```css
/* Respect users who ask for less motion */
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  * { animation-duration: 0.01ms !important; transition-duration: 0.01ms !important; }
}
```

### Sonic identity and AI voices

A short audio mnemonic, a consistent music style or a signature voice can join the identity. If you use AI-generated voice or music, check licenses for commercial use, and clone a real person's voice only with their written consent. Keep a record of which tool, license and consent apply to each audio asset.

### Before/after: a London fitness studio's supporting system

| | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Photos | Glossy stock bodies | Real members (with consent), natural light, warm treatment |
| Icons | Three mismatched free packs | One customized outline set on a 24 px grid |
| Device | None | A diagonal "motion bar" from the logo used to frame photos |
| Motion | Random templates per video | Two-second logo sting, consistent caption animation |

### Summary

Define photography, illustration, icon, graphic device, data, motion and sonic rules so the brand is recognizable even when the logo is not visible.

If they're random, you're invisible. Logo, color and type are the core. But imagery, icons, graphic devices and motion are the supporting cast that people actually see most. In this lecture, you'll learn how to define photography and illustration styles, icon systems, graphic devices, data visualization, motion and sonic identity, and how AI imagery fits in. By the end, your brand will be recognizable without its logo.

lessons.title: What to include in brand guidelines
lessons.body:
### Guidelines exist to be used

Brand guidelines (brand books, style guides) translate your identity into rules and examples other people can follow — employees, freelancers, agencies, printers, partners and influencers. Many guidelines fail because they are long, beautiful PDFs that nobody opens. The best guidelines are **practical, scannable and example-led**.

### Tiered guidelines

Different users need different depth:

| Tier | Audience | Contents |
|---|---|---|
| One-page brand sheet | Everyone, partners, influencers | Logo versions, colors, fonts, key dos/don'ts, contact |
| Core guidelines | Marketing team, freelancers | Full identity rules and examples |
| Extended toolkits | Designers, developers | Templates, tokens, components, motion files |

### Recommended structure

```
1. Brand foundation
   Purpose, audience, positioning, personality, values
2. Verbal identity
   Voice and tone, messaging pillars, vocabulary do/don't, taglines
3. Logo
   Versions, color versions, clear space, minimum sizes, placement, misuse
4. Color
   Palette by role, specs (HEX/RGB/CMYK/spot), ramps, pairings matrix, tokens
5. Typography
   Families, weights, scale, rules, multi-script, fallbacks
6. Imagery
   Photography and illustration style with do/don't examples
7. Graphic elements
   Icons, graphic devices, patterns, data visualization
8. Motion and sound
   Logo animation, motion principles, captions, sonic cues
9. Applications
   Social templates, presentations, documents, website, packaging, signage, merch
10. Accessibility
   Contrast, alt text, captions, inclusive imagery and language
11. Legal and compliance
   Trademark notice, ad disclosure rules, claims guidance, image licenses
12. Resources and contacts
   Asset links, templates, approval process, owner
```

### Writing rules that work

- **Explain the why briefly.** "Use the symbol alone only at small sizes — the wordmark builds name recognition." People follow rules they understand.
- **Show, don't just tell.** Every rule should have a visual example; key rules deserve correct and incorrect examples side by side.
- **Be specific.** "Leave clear space equal to the height of the N" beats "leave plenty of space".
- **Prioritize.** Mark non-negotiables (logo integrity, colors, accessibility) clearly versus flexible areas (layout variety, campaign colors).
- **Use plain language.** Avoid design jargon when non-designers are the audience.

### Guidelines for creators and influencer partners

When brands work with creators, a short **creator brief kit** is more useful than the full guidelines:

- Logo and handle usage, and whether the brand wants logo placement at all (often authentic creator style performs better).
- Key messages and claims that are approved — and claims that are prohibited (health, financial, "guaranteed" results).
- Mandatory disclosure requirements (platform branded-content tools and clear labels such as "#ad" or "Paid partnership" in line with local rules like FTC guidance, the UK CAP Code, and influencer advertising regulations in the UAE and Saudi Arabia).
- Do/don't examples, approval timelines and usage rights.

### Accessibility and inclusion section

Include standards such as minimum contrast (WCAG 2.2 AA as a baseline), alt text practice, captioning for video, avoiding color-only meaning, inclusive and representative imagery, and inclusive language. This turns accessibility from an afterthought into a brand standard.

### Worked example: guidelines for a two-person design studio

The studio creates guidelines for a client café chain expanding from Lahore to Islamabad:

- **One-page sheet** for franchise partners: logo files, colors, two fonts, three don'ts, contact for approvals.
- **Core guidelines (about 30 pages)**: all sections above, with photos from the café's actual shoot.
- **Toolkit**: menu templates, social templates, signage files, uniform embroidery specs, and a bilingual menu layout guide.
- **Governance**: marketing manager as brand owner; a simple approval form for new signage.

### Common mistakes

- Guidelines that are all inspiration and no rules.
- Rules without examples.
- No guidance for real applications people struggle with (menus, email signatures, video captions).
- No accessibility or compliance guidance.

### Making guidelines easy to navigate

However good the content, people will only use guidelines they can navigate quickly. Put a short "start here" page at the front that links to the most common tasks: download the logo, find the colors, open the social templates, request approval. Use consistent page layouts so readers know where to find the rule, the example and the reason on every page. Keep file size manageable so the document opens on a phone, and date every version on its cover so people know whether they are looking at the current rules.

### Hands-on: a brand guidelines template (fill-in)

Use this as the skeleton for a 20–40 page core guideline, a web page per section, or both.

```text
BRAND GUIDELINES — [brand] — v1.0 — [month year] — owner: [name]
0. How to use this guide (who it's for, what's non-negotiable, where assets live)
1. Foundation: purpose · audience · positioning · personality sliders · values
2. Verbal identity: voice principles (do/don't) · messaging pillars · vocabulary
   · bilingual notes (per language, not translations)
3. Logo: variations · color versions · clear space (measured) · minimum sizes
   (px and mm) · placement · 6+ misuse examples
4. Color: roles · specs (HEX/RGB/CMYK/spot) · ramps · approved pairings matrix
   (WCAG 2.2 AA) · tokens
5. Typography: families · weights · scale (digital/social/print) · rules
   · scripts · fallbacks · license notes
6. Imagery: photo and illustration style · do/don't pairs · consent rules
   · AI imagery rules (allowed/banned uses, disclosure)
7. Graphic elements: icons · device · patterns · charts
8. Motion & sound: logo sting · motion principles · captions · sonic cues
9. Applications: social · decks · documents · web · packaging · signage · merch
10. Accessibility: contrast · alt text · captions · inclusive imagery and language
11. Legal: trademark notice · claims · ad and AI disclosure · licenses
12. Resources: asset links · templates · approval tiers · contacts · changelog
```

### Accessibility and AI sections (example wording)

```text
ACCESSIBILITY
- Text must meet WCAG 2.2 AA contrast: 4.5:1 (normal), 3:1 (large). Use the
  pairings matrix in section 4 — no other pairings for text.
- Every published image has alt text; every video has captions.
- Never use color alone to convey meaning.

AI IMAGERY
- Allowed: backgrounds, spot illustrations, concept exploration.
- Not allowed: real customers or staff (without written consent), product
  results, before/afters, news-like scenes, logo creation.
- Realistic AI images: switch on platform AI labels; keep Content Credentials.
- Use only the approved AI style kit and tools listed in Resources.
```

### Before/after: a rule people actually follow

| Before | After |
|---|---|
| "Always give the logo plenty of breathing room." | "Leave clear space equal to the height of the 'N' on every side. Why: it keeps the logo recognizable in busy layouts." + correct/incorrect example images |
| "Use brand colors appropriately." | "Text: navy-900 or white only, from the pairings matrix. Teal-500 is for large shapes, never for text under 24 px." |

### Summary

Structure guidelines from foundation to applications, tier them for different audiences, explain the why, show correct and incorrect examples, and include accessibility, compliance and contacts.
