lessons.title: Delivering assets and living digital guidelines
lessons.body:
### Static PDFs versus living systems

Traditional guidelines are PDF books. They are portable and easy to send, but they go out of date quickly and rarely link directly to assets. Increasingly, brands maintain **living guidelines**: web pages, shared design libraries or brand portals where rules, downloadable assets and templates live together and can be updated.

| Format | Strengths | Weaknesses |
|---|---|---|
| PDF brand book | Easy to share, printable, fixed version | Goes stale, assets separate |
| Web-based guidelines / brand portal | Searchable, updatable, asset downloads | Needs maintenance and hosting |
| Design-tool libraries | Components and styles ready to use | Only for tool users |
| Brand kits in online editors | Non-designers get fonts, colors, logos, templates | Limited rule explanation |

Most small and mid-size brands benefit from a **combination**: a concise PDF or web page for rules, plus a shared library or brand kit for assets and templates.

### Asset delivery checklist

```
Brand asset handover
[ ] Logo pack (all versions, color modes, formats) + README
[ ] Color specs file + tokens (JSON or tool variables)
[ ] Font files or purchase/license links, with license notes
[ ] Icon library (SVG) with naming conventions
[ ] Graphic devices and patterns (vector)
[ ] Photography selects with licenses / releases recorded
[ ] Templates: social, presentation, documents, email signature
[ ] Motion files: logo animation, lower thirds, caption styles
[ ] Guidelines (PDF and/or web) + one-page sheet
[ ] Ownership/license documentation (copyright assignment, font licenses)
```

### Naming and folder conventions

Predictable naming prevents the "which logo is the right one?" problem:

```
brandname_logo_primary_fullcolor_rgb.svg
brandname_logo_symbol_white_rgb.png
brandname_template_ig-carousel_4x5_v1
brandname_colors_tokens_v1.json
```

Include version numbers and dates for templates and guidelines.

### Design tokens and developer handoff

For digital products and websites, provide colors, type scale, spacing and radius values as **tokens** that developers can consume, and align component names between design files and code. Even for simple websites, giving developers exact values prevents "close enough" colors and fonts.

### Templates as guidelines in action

Templates are the most effective way to enforce guidelines, because they embed the rules. Prioritize templates for high-volume items:

- Social posts, carousels, stories and thumbnails.
- Presentation decks and proposals.
- Documents and letterheads.
- Email signatures.
- Event materials and simple ads.

Lock brand elements, name layers clearly, and include placeholder text that explains limits ("Headline — max 6 words").

### Training and onboarding

A brand launch should include a short training session or video:

- Why the brand looks the way it does (strategy recap).
- Where assets live and how to use templates.
- The top five rules and common mistakes.
- How to request new assets or approvals.

Record it so new staff and freelancers can watch later.

### Worked example: a creator-led skincare brand

- **Brand portal**: a simple web page with rules, downloadable logo pack, color tokens, fonts (open-license family) and links to templates.
- **Online editor brand kit**: for the social media assistant, with locked carousel and story templates.
- **Design library**: components for the website and packaging for the freelance designer.
- **Training**: a 15-minute recorded walkthrough; a one-page "top rules" sheet for UGC creators with disclosure requirements.

### Common mistakes

- Handing over a folder of unnamed files.
- Omitting font license information.
- Guidelines with no templates, forcing everyone to design from scratch.
- No training, so the launch fades back into old habits.

### Keeping the toolkit current

A toolkit decays unless someone owns it. Add a version number and a "last updated" date to the portal or PDF, keep a short change log ("v1.2 — new story templates; updated accent color for accessibility"), and announce updates to the people who use the assets. When templates change, archive the previous versions rather than deleting them, so older projects can still be opened, but make it obvious which version is current. A quick monthly check of the most-used templates catches broken fonts, outdated contact details and expired imagery licenses before they spread.

### Hands-on: a living-guidelines setup for a small brand

A practical, low-cost stack (swap in your team's tools):

| Layer | Option | What goes there |
|---|---|---|
| Rules | A web page (Notion, a simple website, or a brand-portal tool such as Frontify) or a concise PDF | The 12 sections, one-page sheet, changelog |
| Design library | Figma team library | Variables (color, spacing), text styles, logo and icon components, templates |
| Non-designer editor | Canva Brand Kit and brand templates (plan-dependent) or Adobe Express brand kits | Logos, colors, fonts, locked templates for staff and partners |
| Files | Shared drive / DAM | Logo pack, fonts and licenses, photography with releases, motion files |
| Code | Token JSON + CSS variables in the website repo | Colors, type scale, spacing, radii |

```text
/Brand_[Name]_v1.0/
  00_README.pdf (what's where, who owns it, version)
  01_Guidelines/ (PDF + link to web version, one-page sheet)
  02_Logo/ (primary, horizontal, stacked, symbol, mono, print, icons) + README
  03_Color/ (spec sheet, pairings matrix, tokens.json)
  04_Type/ (license PDFs, purchase links, fallback stacks)
  05_Icons/ (SVG, naming: icon_[name]_24.svg)
  06_Imagery/ (selects, license log, releases, AI style kit)
  07_Templates/ (social, decks, documents, email signature)
  08_Motion/ (logo sting MP4/Lottie, lower thirds, caption styles)
  09_Legal/ (copyright assignment, font licenses, trademark filings)
```

### Training: a 30-minute launch session outline

1. Why the brand changed (5 min) — strategy in one slide.
2. The top five rules (10 min) — with correct/incorrect examples.
3. Where everything lives (5 min) — live walkthrough of the library and brand kit.
4. Make one real asset together (8 min) — from a template.
5. Who to ask, and how approvals work (2 min).

### Before/after: handover quality

| | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Delivery | Zip file emailed to the founder | Versioned folder + web guidelines + Figma library + Canva brand kit |
| Developer handoff | Screenshots with "roughly this color" | tokens.json and CSS variables |
| Staff use | Stretched logos in office documents | Locked templates and a training session |

### Summary

Combine concise rules with accessible, well-named assets, tokens and templates; deliver license documentation; and train people so the identity is used correctly from day one.

The identity didn't fail. The handover did. In this lecture, you'll learn the difference between static PDFs and living guidelines, what belongs in an asset handover, naming and folder conventions, design tokens for developer handoff, templates as guidelines in action, and how to train people at launch. By the end, you'll deliver a brand that people can actually use from day one.

lessons.title: Brand governance and quality control
lessons.body:
### Consistency does not happen by accident

Even with great guidelines, brands drift. New staff create their own flyers, partners stretch logos, campaigns introduce one-off colors, and templates get edited until they break. **Governance** is the set of roles, processes and checks that keep the brand consistent while still allowing it to evolve.

### Roles

| Role | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| Brand owner | Final decisions, guideline updates, exceptions |
| Brand champions | Help teams apply the brand in their area (sales, regional offices) |
| Creators of assets | Designers, marketers, freelancers, partners — follow the system |
| Approvers | Review high-visibility or unusual work before publishing |

In a small business, the founder or marketing lead may hold all of these roles; the point is that someone clearly owns the brand.

### Approval tiers

Not everything needs approval. Use risk-based tiers:

```
Tier 1 — Self-serve (no approval):
  Social posts from approved templates, email signatures, standard documents
Tier 2 — Quick review:
  New campaign visuals, partner co-branding, paid ads, influencer content
Tier 3 — Full review:
  Signage, packaging, logo changes, new sub-brands, anything legal/regulated
```

Tiered approvals keep speed high while protecting what matters.

### Brand review checklist

```
[ ] Correct logo version, clear space, minimum size
[ ] Approved colors and accessible text pairings
[ ] Brand typefaces and scale
[ ] Imagery matches style; licenses and consents documented
[ ] Voice and tone on-brand; claims approved and supportable
[ ] Disclosures present for paid/affiliate content
[ ] Accessibility: contrast, alt text, captions
[ ] Correct templates used; no placeholder text
```

### Managing exceptions and evolution

Guidelines should evolve with real use. Set up:

- **An exceptions log:** when someone needs to break a rule (a partner's co-branding requirement, a special campaign), record the decision and why.
- **A feedback channel:** where users can report problems ("the template breaks with long names").
- **Scheduled reviews:** for example twice a year, update templates and guidelines based on the log and feedback.
- **Versioning:** date and version guidelines; archive old templates so they are not reused.

### Campaign flexibility

Campaigns often need freshness. Allow **controlled flexibility**: a campaign may introduce a seasonal color, illustration style or photography theme, provided core assets (logo, signature color, typefaces, graphic device) remain. Seasonal campaigns such as Ramadan, Eid, Diwali, Christmas, back-to-school or national days can use special palettes and motifs while clearly remaining the same brand — and should be designed with cultural knowledge and respect.

### Measuring brand consistency and health

You cannot measure everything, but you can track signals:

- **Consistency audits:** periodically sample recent touchpoints and score them against the checklist.
- **Template adoption:** how much content is produced from official templates.
- **Recognition feedback:** ask customers in surveys or interviews what they associate with the brand, or run simple recognition tests with brand cues shown without the name.
- **Qualitative feedback:** from sales teams, partners and customers.

### Worked example: a growing agency with remote freelancers

Problem: ten freelancers across Pakistan, the UAE and the UK produce client-facing decks and social content that look inconsistent.

Governance fix:

1. The creative director becomes brand owner; one senior designer is the brand champion.
2. Locked deck and social templates shared in the team's design tool.
3. Tier 1 for template-based work; Tier 2 for new campaign visuals with a 24-hour review turnaround.
4. Quarterly audit of 20 random outputs against the checklist; results shared with the team.
5. Exceptions log reviewed at each quarterly guidelines update.

### Common mistakes

- No clear owner.
- Approving everything (slow) or nothing (drift).
- Treating guidelines as fixed forever.
- Punitive "brand police" culture that discourages people from asking for help.

### A lightweight governance rhythm for small teams

Governance does not need committees. For a creator business or small agency, a simple rhythm works well: a weekly five-minute glance at everything published that week, a monthly review of template requests and problems, and a quarterly audit and guidelines update. Keep the process visible in a shared document so everyone knows how to get help. The aim is to make the right thing the easy thing — people follow the brand when the templates are good and the answers are quick.

### Hands-on: a brand audit scorecard (run quarterly)

Sample 20 recent assets across channels and score each line 0–2 (0 = off-brand, 1 = partly, 2 = on-brand).

```text
BRAND CONSISTENCY AUDIT — quarter: ____  sample: 20 assets  auditor: ____
Logo: correct version, clear space, minimum size          0 1 2
Color: approved palette and pairings                      0 1 2
Type: brand fonts, scale, rules                           0 1 2
Imagery: style, licenses/consents, AI rules followed      0 1 2
Voice: on-brand tone; claims approved                     0 1 2
Templates: used where available; no placeholders          0 1 2
Accessibility: contrast, alt text, captions               0 1 2
Disclosure: #ad / paid partnership / AI labels as needed   0 1 2
Score per asset: __/16   Channel average: __   Trend vs last quarter: __
Top 3 fixes (templates, training, guideline updates): __________
```

### Governance for AI-assisted content

Add AI to the governance plan explicitly:

- **Who may use which tools** (approved tools list, plans with suitable data controls).
- **What needs approval** — for example, any realistic AI image goes to Tier 2 review.
- **Records** — prompt logs and Content Credentials kept for AI-assisted assets.
- **Disclosure** — who switches on platform labels and writes the caption note.

### Simple RACI for a small team

| Activity | Brand owner | Designer | Marketing lead | Freelancers |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Guideline updates | A | R | C | I |
| Tier 2 approvals | A | C | R | I |
| Template maintenance | A | R | C | I |
| Quarterly audit | A | R | R | I |

R = responsible, A = accountable, C = consulted, I = informed.

### Before/after: a growing agency with remote freelancers

| | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Approvals | Everything to the founder, bottlenecks | Three tiers; templates are self-serve |
| Drift | Each freelancer "improved" templates | Locked masters; exceptions log |
| Evidence | Opinions about consistency | Quarterly audit score per channel |

### Summary

Assign ownership, use risk-based approval tiers and a review checklist, log exceptions, review guidelines regularly, allow controlled campaign flexibility, and audit consistency over time.

lessons.body:
### Social is where most people meet the brand

For creators and many small businesses, social feeds and short-form video are the main touchpoints. Yet social is where identities break most often: content is produced quickly, by many people, in many formats, often reacting to trends. The goal is **recognizable, not identical** — a system flexible enough for daily content yet consistent enough to build memory.

### The social identity toolkit

| Element | What to define |
|---|---|
| Profile | Symbol-only avatar, cover/banner layouts, bio voice |
| Post templates | Quote, tip, announcement, carousel cover/content/CTA |
| Story/vertical templates | Announcement, Q&A, poll, behind the scenes |
| Thumbnails | Layout families, type treatment, face/object framing |
| Video | Intro sting (optional), lower thirds, caption style, end card |
| Color use | Which palette colors for backgrounds; accent rules |
| Photography | Style, treatment preset, framing rules |
| Voice | Caption style, emoji use, hashtag approach, CTA phrasing |

### Recognizable at thumbnail size

Brand cues on social must survive tiny sizes and fast scrolling:

- **Color world** — a consistent background color family is among the strongest feed cues.
- **Typography** — a distinctive headline treatment repeated across covers.
- **Graphic device** — a signature frame, underline or shape.
- **Face and framing** — for creators, consistent framing and expressions are brand assets.
- **Layout families** — two or three layouts used repeatedly rather than a new layout each post.

Logos are often less important on social than people think; a large logo on every post can make content feel like an ad and reduce engagement. A small, consistent placement or symbol watermark is often enough — and many creator-led brands use none on organic posts.

### Trends versus brand

Trends (formats, audio, memes) can drive reach. Participate in a branded way:

1. **Filter:** does the trend fit the brand's personality and values? Does it involve sensitive topics?
2. **Adapt:** use the trend's format with your colors, captions, voice and point of view.
3. **Check rights:** trending audio may be licensed only for personal accounts; business accounts often have restricted music libraries. Check platform rules for commercial use.
4. **Keep the core:** caption style, color treatment and voice should still be recognizable.

### Video identity details

- **Captions:** brand font (or a close legible match), consistent size, position within safe zones, a highlight color for key words.
- **Lower thirds:** name/title bars using brand colors and graphic device.
- **Intro:** on short-form, long intros cost viewers; use a very short sting or none, and put branding in captions and framing instead.
- **End card:** consistent layout with CTA and handle.
- **Sound:** consistent music style or sonic sting where appropriate and licensed.

### Worked example: a Karachi-based food creator

Challenge: posts look random — different fonts, colors and edit styles.

Social system:

- Color world: warm terracotta and cream backgrounds, with a mustard accent.
- Two carousel layouts (recipe steps, restaurant review) and one cover template with the dish photo top and bold title bottom.
- Reels: captions in a rounded bold sans, cream text with terracotta highlight on key words; consistent overhead shot for cooking; a two-second sizzle sound as sonic cue.
- Thumbnails/covers: dish close-up, creator's hand or face in frame, two-to-three word title.
- Voice: warm, mixes Urdu and English naturally, no exaggerated claims about restaurants; sponsored reviews clearly disclosed.

Result: followers recognize posts in the feed before seeing the handle.

### Channel consistency matrix

```
Asset/cue        IG   TikTok  YouTube  LinkedIn  Website  Email
Symbol avatar    ✓    ✓       ✓        ✓         favicon  ✓
Color world     ✓    ✓       ✓        ✓         ✓        ✓
Headline type    ✓    captions ✓ thumbs ✓       ✓        ✓ (fallback)
Graphic device   ✓    ✓       ✓        ✓         ✓        ✓
Voice            casual casual casual   more formal ✓      ✓
```

Use a matrix like this to see where cues are missing and where tone flexes by channel.

### Common mistakes

- A new layout for every post.
- Large logos on every organic post.
- Trend content that abandons all brand cues.
- Different profile pictures across platforms.

### Hands-on: a social identity kit build list (Figma + Canva)

```text
SOCIAL IDENTITY KIT — [brand] v1
Profile:     symbol avatar (circle-safe) · banner/cover per platform · bio voice line
Templates:   post (quote, tip, announcement) · carousel (cover, content, CTA)
             · story (announcement, Q&A, poll) · Reel/TikTok cover · YouTube thumbnail family
Video:       2-second logo sting · lower third · caption style (font, size, box, position)
             · end card · safe-zone overlay per platform
Color use:   background family (e.g. warm sand 60%) · accent only on key element
Photography: preset name · framing rules · consent rules
AI content:  approved AI style kit · allowed uses · label rules
Voice:       caption structure · emoji policy · hashtag policy · CTA phrasing
Disclosure:  paid partnership tool + "Ad" at the start + on-image label for paid posts
```

**Working sizes to template** (verify in each platform's help center before building): 1080 × 1350 (feed 4:5), 1080 × 1920 (stories, Reels, TikTok, Shorts), 16:9 YouTube thumbnails (YouTube currently recommends up to 3840 × 2160), and platform-specific banners. Keep the profile grid preview (3:4 on Instagram) and each app's UI overlays in mind.

### Caption and subtitle style spec (video)

```text
Font: Brand Sans Bold · Size: ~5-6% of frame height · Max 2 lines, ≤ 32 characters/line
Box: 80% opacity brand-navy, 12 px radius · Position: lower-middle, above the app's caption/UI zone
Emphasis: key word in accent color (one per line max) · Always on: yes (sound-off viewing)
Arabic/Urdu: right-aligned, script-appropriate font, +15% line height
```

| | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Thumbnails | Different fonts and colors every video | One layout family: dish close-up, two-word headline, saffron chip |
| Video | No intro; random caption styles | 1-second sting; consistent captions; end card with symbol |
| Grid | Random filters | One warm preset; cream background family |
| Recognition | Viewers didn't know it was her until the name appeared | Recognizable from the thumbnail alone |

### Summary

Build a social toolkit with templates, color world, type treatment, graphic device and video rules; aim for recognizable rather than identical; and join trends in a branded, rights-aware way.

lessons.title: Web, documents, packaging and physical touchpoints
lessons.body:
### Beyond the feed

A brand is judged at every touchpoint: the website a lead visits after a post, the proposal a client receives, the invoice, the product packaging, the shop sign, the uniform, the event stand. Inconsistency at any of these moments can undermine trust built elsewhere.

### Website and digital products

The website is often the brand's most complete expression. Priorities:

- **Tokens and components:** apply colors, type scale, spacing and radii via tokens so the site matches the design system.
- **Accessibility:** WCAG 2.2 AA contrast, keyboard access, alt text, captions, clear focus states. Accessibility is increasingly a legal expectation for websites in many jurisdictions.
- **Performance:** optimize images and fonts (limit the number of font files and weights), because slow pages hurt experience.
- **Favicon and app icon:** use the symbol, simplified for tiny sizes.
- **Social preview images (Open Graph):** branded templates for link previews, so shared links look consistent.
- **Multi-language:** right-to-left layouts for Arabic and Urdu need proper mirroring, not just translated text.

### Documents: proposals, decks, invoices

For agencies and freelancers, documents are high-stakes brand moments.

```
Document toolkit
- Proposal template (cover, about, scope, timeline, pricing, terms)
- Pitch/presentation deck (title, section, content, case study, quote, closing)
- Case study layout
- Invoice and quote templates
- Letterhead and report template
- Email signature (text + small logo; avoid large images)
```

Tips: use the brand fallback fonts where recipients may not have brand fonts; export PDFs to lock layout; keep accessible reading order for PDFs where possible.

### Packaging

Packaging adds physical constraints:

- **Materials and printing** change color appearance (kraft paper, metallic foils, fabric). Always proof on the actual material.
- **Regulatory information** — ingredients, warnings, halal certification marks, barcodes, recycling symbols, origin — must fit legibly and meet local labeling requirements. Leave space in the design system for it.
- **Hierarchy on shelf** — brand recognition, product type, variant and key benefit, readable from a distance.
- **Variant systems** — colors or patterns that distinguish flavors or sizes while keeping the brand block consistent.
- **Unboxing** — for e-commerce and creator products, the inside experience (tissue, inserts, thank-you cards) is a content opportunity.

### Signage, environments and merchandise

- **Signage:** test legibility from viewing distances; consider lighting (backlit, day/night); follow local signage regulations and, where required, bilingual signage rules (for example, Arabic is commonly required or prioritized on signage in Gulf markets — check local municipality rules).
- **Environments:** colors, materials and wayfinding in shops, studios or event stands.
- **Merchandise and uniforms:** embroidery and screen printing need simplified, one-color-capable logos and minimum sizes; test on fabric.

### Consistency without sameness

Different touchpoints need different expressions:

| Touchpoint | Expression |
|---|---|
| Social | Expressive, playful, trend-aware |
| Website | Clear, structured, conversion-focused |
| Proposals | Professional, confident, concise |
| Packaging | Bold on the outside, delightful inside |
| Signage | Simple and legible at distance |

The same core assets appear everywhere; intensity and tone vary.

### Worked example: a small agency's client journey

1. **Discovery:** a LinkedIn carousel in brand templates.
2. **Website:** matching colors and type; case studies in consistent layouts.
3. **Call booking:** branded scheduling page with logo and color.
4. **Proposal:** branded PDF, clear structure, consistent tone.
5. **Onboarding:** welcome pack PDF and branded project workspace.
6. **Invoices:** clean branded template with payment details.
7. **Delivery:** reports and decks in brand templates.

Mapping the journey revealed the invoice and onboarding pack were unbranded, which the agency fixed in a day using templates.

### Common mistakes

- A beautiful social presence but an off-brand, inaccessible website.
- Proposals built from scratch each time.
- Not proofing packaging on the real material.
- Leaving no space for regulatory information on packaging.

### Budgeting for touchpoints

Physical touchpoints cost far more to change than digital ones, so plan them with the future in mind. Before printing large runs of packaging or signage, confirm the identity is final, the regulatory text is approved and the files have been proofed. For small businesses, printing smaller batches at first reduces the cost of mistakes. Keep editable master files and supplier specifications (materials, finishes, color references) in the asset library so reorders match previous runs instead of drifting over time.

### Hands-on: mockups that sell the system (and stay honest)

Clients approve identities faster when they see them in real contexts. A practical workflow:

1. **Pick contexts from the touchpoint list** — website hero, proposal cover, invoice, packaging front, shop sign, uniform, event stand.
2. **Use editable mockup templates**: Photoshop mockups with smart objects (double-click the smart object, paste the design, save — the scene updates), or Figma frames with image fills and perspective set up by the mockup's author.
3. **Check licenses**: many mockup templates are free for personal use only; commercial client presentations may need a paid license.
4. **Label visualizations**: if a mockup scene is AI-generated or the placement isn't real (a billboard you haven't booked), label it "concept visualization".
5. **Print-test critical items**: packaging colors and small type need physical proofs, not just mockups.

### Web essentials checklist

```text
[ ] Tokens drive colors, type scale, spacing, radii (no hard-coded hex)
[ ] WCAG 2.2 AA: contrast, keyboard access, visible focus, 24×24 px min targets, alt text, captions
[ ] Fonts: 2-4 font files max; font-display strategy; fallbacks specified
[ ] Favicon (SVG + PNG/ICO), apple-touch-icon 180×180, manifest icons
[ ] Open Graph / social preview template ~1200×630 with centered text
[ ] RTL: dir="rtl" layouts properly mirrored for Arabic/Urdu pages
[ ] Images: modern formats (WebP/AVIF) with sensible compression
```

### Document toolkit (freelancers and agencies)

| Document | Brand job | Template must include |
|---|---|---|
| Proposal | Win trust | Cover, strategy page, process, pricing table, terms |
| Deck | Explain clearly | Title, section, content, data, quote, closing slides |
| Invoice | Look professional | Logo, legal details, clear totals, payment terms |
| Contract | Feel reliable | Consistent type, numbered clauses, signature block |
| Email signature | Reinforce, lightly | Name, role, horizontal logo (small PNG), one link |

### Before/after: a small agency's client journey

| Touchpoint | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Proposal | Word default template | Branded proposal template with strategy page |
| Invoice | Accounting-software default | Branded invoice template (logo, palette, type) |
| Website | Brand teal fails as link color | Accessible teal-700 for links; tokens in CSS |
| Office sign | Old logo | New sign scheduled in the phased rollout |

### Summary

Map the full customer journey, apply tokens and templates to web and documents, respect physical and regulatory constraints for packaging and signage, and vary intensity by touchpoint while keeping core assets constant.

They request a proposal, which arrives as a default word-processor document. They sign, and the invoice comes from accounting software with no logo at all. Each step chips away at the trust the carousel built. A brand is judged at every touchpoint, not just the pretty ones. In this lecture, you'll learn how identity applies to websites and digital products, documents like proposals, decks and invoices, packaging, signage, environments and merchandise, how to use mockups honestly, and how to budget for touchpoints. By the end, you'll map a whole customer journey and fix its weakest point.

lessons.title: Co-branding, partnerships and creator collaborations
lessons.body:
### When two brands meet

Collaborations — sponsorships, creator partnerships, co-branded products, events, charity campaigns — put your identity next to someone else's. Done well, they transfer trust and reach. Done badly, they confuse audiences or make one brand look subordinate.

### Types of partnership and visual hierarchy

| Partnership | Typical visual relationship |
|---|---|
| Equal co-brand (joint product) | Both logos at equal visual weight, separated by a divider or "×" |
| Sponsor of an event or creator | Host/event brand leads; sponsor shown as "Presented by" or "In partnership with" |
| Endorsed sub-brand | Sub-brand leads; parent brand endorses ("by Brand") |
| Creator paid partnership | Creator's style leads; brand appears naturally, with clear disclosure |
| Supplier/client showcase | Client logos in a consistent monochrome grid, with permission |

### Co-branded lockup rules

Define how your logo appears alongside others:

- **Equal optical size** (not identical measurements — wordmarks and symbols need visual balancing).
- **Clear space** between logos at least equal to your standard clear-space rule.
- **Separator**: a vertical line, "×", or "+" — defined in guidelines.
- **Color**: when backgrounds conflict, use one-color versions of both logos.
- **Order**: often the host or lead partner first (left in LTR layouts, right in RTL layouts); agree this in writing.

### Permission and legal basics

- **Never use another brand's logo without permission** in a way that implies partnership, endorsement or affiliation. Showing client logos in a portfolio typically also needs permission (and may be restricted by NDAs).
- **Follow their guidelines** — partners have their own logo usage rules.
- **Contracts** should cover logo usage, approvals, content rights, duration and what happens after the partnership ends.

### Creator partnerships: authenticity plus compliance

Brand teams often over-brand creator content, which makes it feel like an ad and can underperform. Best practice:

- Brief creators on key messages, claims and do/don'ts, then let them create in their own style.
- Use the platform's branded-content or paid-partnership tools where available, plus clear labels in the content.
- Follow disclosure rules in each market — for example the FTC's Endorsement Guides in the US, the CAP Code and ASA guidance in the UK, the UAE's media regulations on advertising by influencers (including licensing requirements for influencers), and Saudi Arabia's rules for advertising by social media influencers. Rules evolve; check current requirements.
- Agree **usage rights**: can the brand reuse the content as ads (whitelisting/"Spark"-style ads), on its website, for how long, in which territories?

### Protecting your identity in partnerships

As a brand or creator, provide partners with:

```
Partner kit
- Logo files (full color, one color, reversed) + lockup examples
- One-page usage rules (clear space, don'ts)
- Approved descriptions of the brand (short and long)
- Approved imagery or headshots
- Approval contact and turnaround time
```

### Worked example: a creator × brand collaboration

A UK-based fitness creator partners with a sportswear brand for a limited capsule collection.

- **Product labels:** equal co-brand lockup — creator wordmark × brand logo, balanced optically, one-color on fabric tags.
- **Launch content:** creator's own filming style and captions; sportswear logo appears on product naturally; "Paid partnership" label and "#ad" at the start of captions.
- **Brand's channels:** brand-led layouts with creator's name as "designed with"; creator approved all uses.
- **Contract:** 12-month usage rights for paid ads in agreed markets; approvals within 48 hours; logo usage ends after the capsule sells through.

### Common mistakes

- Using partner logos without permission or outside their guidelines.
- Unbalanced lockups that make one partner look less important unintentionally.
- Over-branded creator content that feels like a banner ad.
- Missing or hidden disclosure.

### After the partnership ends

Plan the end of a collaboration at the start. Contracts should state when each party must stop using the other's logo, whether existing content can stay online, and whether paid ads featuring the creator must be switched off by a certain date. Keep a simple register of active partnerships, their usage rights and end dates, and review it monthly. This prevents awkward situations where a former partner's logo remains on your website or an ad keeps running after the rights have expired.

### Hands-on: build a partner kit and co-brand lockups in Figma

1. Create a component `Lockup/Equal` with an auto-layout row: your logo, a separator (vertical line or ×), the partner logo slot. Set the gap to your clear-space value on both sides of the separator.
2. Create `Lockup/Presented-by`: the host brand large, then "Presented by" in your label style, then the sponsor logo slot at a smaller defined ratio.
3. Add variants for light, dark and one-color backgrounds.
4. **Optical balancing:** place both logos, then scale the partner logo until they *look* equal (compare visual weight, not bounding boxes). Note the final ratio in the kit.
5. Publish and export a partner kit folder.

```text
PARTNER KIT — [brand] v1
/logos     (primary, horizontal, symbol; full color, white, black; SVG + PNG)
/lockups   (equal, presented-by, in-partnership-with; light/dark/one-color)
/rules.pdf (clear space, minimum sizes, don'ts, approval contact, turnaround)
/creator-brief.pdf (handle to tag, tone, do/don't content, claims allowed/banned,
                    disclosure: paid partnership tool + "Ad" first + on-image label,
                    AI rules: no AI-generated results/testimonials)
/examples  (approved co-branded posts)
```

### Disclosure essentials for creator partnerships (check each market's current rules)

- **US:** the FTC's Endorsement Guides expect clear and conspicuous disclosure of material connections (payment, free products, family ties).
- **UK:** the ASA/CAP rules require ads to be obviously identifiable — "Ad" or "#ad" up front is the common approach.
- **UAE and Saudi Arabia:** regulators have specific rules and licensing or permit requirements for influencer advertising; confirm current requirements before campaigns.
- **Everywhere:** use the platform's paid-partnership tool as well as caption and on-image disclosure; never fake testimonials or use AI to simulate results.

### Before/after: a creator × brand collaboration

| | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Visual | Creator told to "use our brand colors" — looked like an ad, performance dropped | Creator's style leads; brand appears naturally via product, handle tag and one brand color accent |
| Disclosure | "#sp" at the end of the hashtags | Paid partnership tool + "Ad" first + small on-image label |
| Logo | Stretched logo from a screenshot | Approved lockup from the partner kit |
| Afterwards | Old campaign assets still used by the creator a year later | Contract defines usage period; assets archived after it ends |

### Summary

Choose the right visual hierarchy for the partnership type, define co-brand lockup rules, get permission and contracts in place, balance authenticity with clear disclosure in creator work, and supply partners with a simple kit.

lessons.title: Refresh or rebrand? Making the right call
lessons.body:
### Change is expensive — and sometimes essential

Every identity eventually faces pressure to change: the business evolves, the market shifts, the design looks dated, or a merger happens. The question is not "should we change?" but "how much, and why?"

### The spectrum of change

| Level | What changes | When it fits |
|---|---|---|
| Housekeeping | Fix inconsistencies, tidy files, add templates | The identity is fine but applied badly |
| Refresh / evolution | Modernize logo details, update type, expand palette, refine system | The brand is recognized but looks dated or fails digitally |
| Repositioning with new identity | Strategy changes; visuals change substantially | New audience, new offer, new price point |
| Full rebrand (possibly new name) | Name, logo, entire system | Merger, legal issues, reputational damage, name that no longer fits |

Many businesses that think they need a rebrand actually need housekeeping or a refresh.

### Legitimate reasons to change

- **Strategy has changed:** a freelancer becomes an agency; a local shop expands to new cities or countries; a creator moves from entertainment to education.
- **The identity fails functionally:** unreadable at small sizes, doesn't work on mobile, no bilingual version, inaccessible colors.
- **Legal problems:** trademark conflicts, a name that can't be protected in new markets.
- **Mergers or acquisitions.**
- **Reputational reasons:** though a new logo alone won't fix a real problem — the underlying issue must be addressed.
- **Looks genuinely dated** in ways that undermine credibility with the target audience.

### Weak reasons to change

- A new leader wants to "make their mark".
- The team is bored of the logo (internal teams tire of assets far sooner than customers notice them).
- A competitor rebranded.
- Following a design trend.

### Brand equity: know what you would lose

Before deciding, identify which assets carry recognition:

```
Equity assessment
Asset                 Recognition (H/M/L)   Evidence                  Keep / evolve / drop
Name                  ______                 search, mentions          ______
Signature color      ______                 customer interviews        ______
Logo symbol           ______                 recognition tests          ______
Typography            ______                 ______                     ______
Graphic device        ______                 ______                     ______
Tagline / sound       ______                 ______                     ______
```

Evidence can come from customer interviews, simple recognition tests (show a cue without the name and ask who it belongs to), social comments, search behavior and sales team feedback.

Assets with high recognition should usually be **evolved, not discarded**.

### Decision framework

Ask in order:

1. Has the **strategy** changed? If no, lean toward housekeeping or refresh.
2. Does the identity **function** across today's channels (mobile, video, small sizes, accessibility, languages)? If no, at least a refresh.
3. Are there **legal** constraints? If yes, a name or logo change may be unavoidable.
4. What **equity** exists? Protect high-recognition assets.
5. What can the business **afford** to change (signage, packaging, vehicles, uniforms, digital)? Plan phasing.

### Worked example: a creator's refresh

A tech reviewer's channel has grown from a hobby to a media business with a team. The logo is a low-resolution gaming-style emblem; thumbnails use four different fonts; the audience recognizes the creator's yellow backgrounds and catchphrase.

Decision: **refresh**, not full rebrand.

- Keep: the name, the yellow (now defined as a precise color with an accessible ramp), the catchphrase.
- Evolve: redraw the emblem into a clean monogram and wordmark that works at 32 px.
- Add: a type system (one headline family), thumbnail templates, lower thirds, and a sponsor kit.

Audience response is positive because the brand still feels familiar — just sharper.

### Common mistakes

- Treating a rebrand as a cure for business problems.
- Discarding recognized assets without evidence.
- Underestimating the physical rollout cost.
- Changing because insiders are bored.

### Talking about change with clients

When a client asks for a rebrand, begin with questions rather than proposals: What has changed in the business? What problems does the current identity cause, and where? What do customers already recognize? Framing the conversation around evidence protects the client from spending money on unnecessary change and positions you as an adviser rather than a supplier of logos. Sometimes the most valuable recommendation you can make is a refresh plus better templates — and clients remember that honesty.

### Hands-on: brand equity assessment

Before recommending any change, score what the brand already owns. Use evidence: customer interviews, reviews, social comments, search terms and (for larger brands) recognition surveys.

```text
EQUITY ASSESSMENT — [brand]
Asset                  Recognized by customers?  Distinctive vs competitors?  Functional today?  Decision
                       (0-2, evidence)            (0-2)                        (0-2)
Name                   _                          _                            _                  keep / evolve / replace
Logo symbol            _                          _                            _
Wordmark               _                          _                            _
Signature color        _                          _                            _
Typography             _                          _                            _
Graphic device/pattern _                          _                            _
Mascot/character       _                          _                            _
Voice/tagline          _                          _                            _
Rule: score 5-6 → keep (refine at most); 3-4 → evolve; 0-2 → candidate to replace
```

### Decision framework (quick version)

| If… | Then consider… |
|---|---|
| The identity is fine but applied badly | Housekeeping: templates, guidelines, governance |
| Recognized but dated or failing digitally (small sizes, dark mode, accessibility, bilingual) | Refresh / evolution |
| Strategy has changed (audience, offer, price point, markets) | Repositioning with a new identity |
| Merger, legal conflict, reputational damage or a name that no longer fits | Full rebrand, possibly a new name |

### Before/after: a creator's refresh

| | Before | After (refresh, not rebrand) |
|---|---|---|
| Logo | Thin script wordmark, unreadable at avatar size | Same name, redrawn bolder wordmark + monogram for small sizes |
| Color | Purple kept (followers recognize it), but light purple text failed contrast | Same purple family; darker purple for text; pairings matrix |
| Type | Five fonts over three years | One headline family + one body family |
| Audience reaction | — | "Looks more grown-up, still you" (typical feedback when equity is kept) |

A useful test: **would loyal customers still recognize you?** If a change fails that test, you need a strong strategic reason for it.

### Summary

Place the change on the spectrum from housekeeping to full rebrand, separate strong from weak reasons, assess equity with evidence, and use a structured decision framework before committing.

scenes.narration: Here's a conversation that happens in a lot of businesses. The founder is bored of the logo, a competitor just launched a slick new look, and someone says, let's rebrand. It sounds exciting. It's also expensive, risky, and often unnecessary. Some of the most famous rebrand failures happened because a company threw away the colors and shapes customers loved, and customers hated the change. Other businesses really do need change, because their strategy has moved or their identity simply doesn't work on a phone. In this lecture, you'll learn the spectrum of change, legitimate and weak reasons to change, how to assess brand equity, and a decision framework. By the end, you'll recommend the right level of change, with evidence.

scenes.narration: Why is this decision so important? Because brand equity takes years to build and minutes to lose. Every time a customer sees your color, your symbol or your wordmark alongside a good experience, the association gets stronger. Change those cues, and some of that memory resets. That doesn't mean never change. It means change on purpose, by the right amount. Think of a favorite restaurant that renovates. If it keeps the signature dish, the warm lighting and the friendly staff, and fixes the broken chairs, regulars are delighted. If it becomes a completely different restaurant with the same name, regulars feel lost. The question isn't whether to change. It's how much, and why.

scenes.narration: Here's the spectrum of change. Housekeeping: fix inconsistencies, tidy files and add templates, when the identity is fine but applied badly. A refresh, or evolution: modernize logo details, update type, expand the palette and refine the system, when the brand is recognized but looks dated or fails digitally. Repositioning with a new identity: when strategy changes, like a new audience, offer or price point, and the visuals change substantially. And a full rebrand, possibly with a new name: for mergers, legal problems, reputational damage, or a name that no longer fits. Here's the key idea. Many businesses that think they need a rebrand actually need housekeeping or a refresh.

scenes.narration: Legitimate reasons to change include: the strategy has changed, like a freelancer becoming an agency, a local shop expanding to new cities or countries, or a creator moving from entertainment to education. The identity fails functionally: unreadable at small sizes, broken on mobile, no bilingual version, or inaccessible colors. Legal problems, like a trademark conflict. A merger or acquisition. Or reputational damage that the old identity can't escape. Weak reasons include: the founder is bored, a competitor rebranded, a new marketing manager wants to leave a mark, or a trend looks exciting. Remember, the people inside a business see the identity a thousand times more than customers do. Boredom inside isn't fatigue outside.

scenes.narration: Before deciding, assess brand equity, meaning what the brand already owns in people's minds. Use evidence: customer interviews, reviews, social comments, search terms, and recognition surveys for larger brands. For each asset, the name, the symbol, the wordmark, the signature color, typography, a graphic device, a mascot and the voice, score three things. Is it recognized by customers? Is it distinctive compared with competitors? And does it work functionally today? High scores mean keep it, and refine it at most. Middle scores mean evolve it. Low scores make it a candidate to replace. This turns a gut feeling into a defensible recommendation.

lessons.title: Running a rebrand project and presenting the work
lessons.body:
### A rebrand is a change-management project

Designing new visuals is only part of a rebrand. The project also involves stakeholders, legal checks, communication, budget and a rollout plan. Treat it like a project with phases and decision points.

### Typical phases

| Phase | Key activities | Output |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Discovery | Stakeholder interviews, audit, equity assessment, competitor landscape | Findings report |
| 2. Strategy | Positioning, personality, architecture decisions | Approved strategy and brief |
| 3. Exploration | Territories, concepts, name exploration if needed | Chosen direction |
| 4. Design development | Logo system, color, type, supporting elements | Core identity |
| 5. Validation | Legal checks, accessibility checks, customer feedback, application tests | Refined identity |
| 6. System and guidelines | Guidelines, templates, tokens, asset packs | Toolkit |
| 7. Rollout | Phased implementation, launch communication, training | Live brand |

Small projects compress these phases, but skipping them entirely (especially discovery and validation) creates risk.

### Stakeholder management

- **Identify decision makers early.** Know who approves at each phase, and avoid adding new decision makers late.
- **Share the "why" first.** Present research and strategy before visuals, so reviews are anchored to objectives.
- **Limit opinions from large groups.** Gather input broadly in discovery, but keep design decisions with a small team.

### Presenting identity work

A strong presentation structure:

1. **Recap** the objectives, audience and strategy (one or two slides).
2. **Show the idea** — the concept in one sentence.
3. **Reveal the logo** in black and white, then color.
4. **Show the system** — colors, type, graphic device, imagery.
5. **Show it in use** — realistic mock-ups of key touchpoints (social feed, website, packaging, sign, app icon).
6. **Connect back** — how the identity meets each objective.
7. **Next steps** — refinements, validation, rollout.

### Handling feedback

Useful ways to guide feedback:

- Ask reviewers to respond against the brief: "Which objective does this meet or miss?"
- Separate **first reactions** (natural discomfort with anything new) from considered feedback after a day.
- Translate vague feedback: "Make it pop" → "Do you feel the logo lacks contrast or energy? Which touchpoint?"
- Avoid design by committee: combining everyone's preferences produces bland compromises.

Remember that new identities often feel uncomfortable at first simply because they are unfamiliar.

### Validation before launch

```
Validation checklist
[ ] Trademark search/clearance for name and logo in key markets
[ ] Domain names and social handles secured
[ ] Accessibility: contrast pairings, small-size legibility
[ ] Multi-language checks (meaning, script rendering)
[ ] Cultural review in each key market
[ ] Customer feedback sessions (qualitative) with target audience
[ ] Production tests: print proofs, embroidery, signage samples
```

### Legal and IP checklist (principle level)

- Clear the name and logo in relevant classes and countries (use a professional for significant investments).
- Ensure copyright in all new assets is assigned to the business.
- Confirm licenses for fonts, images, icons and music used in the system.
- Plan how to handle old trademarks (keep, let lapse, or maintain for protection).

### Worked example: freelancer to agency

A solo designer in Islamabad is becoming a four-person agency serving clients in the Gulf.

- Discovery: interviews with five past clients revealed they valued "calm, reliable delivery" above "creativity".
- Strategy: position as a dependable brand-and-content partner for growing Gulf businesses.
- Exploration: three territories; the "calm precision" territory chosen.
- Design: new name (the founder's personal name no longer fit a team), bilingual wordmark, deep blue signature color, precise grid device.
- Validation: trademark searches in Pakistan and the UAE, native Arabic review of the wordmark, feedback from three prospective clients.
- Presentation: strategy first, then mock-ups of proposal, LinkedIn page and website.

### Common mistakes

- Skipping discovery and going straight to logos.
- Presenting visuals without the strategy.
- Letting too many people vote on design.
- Launching before legal clearance and handles are secured.

### Timelines and budgets

Be realistic about time. Even a small rebrand involves research, several review rounds, legal checks and production lead times, and each approval step depends on stakeholders' availability. Build buffers into the plan, agree the number of revision rounds in the contract, and flag which decisions are on the critical path (for example, name clearance must be complete before signage is ordered). Clear timelines reduce pressure to skip validation steps at the end.

### Hands-on: rebrand project plan template

```text
REBRAND PLAN — [brand] — sponsor: ____ — brand owner: ____ — agency/lead: ____
Phase            Weeks   Decision maker(s)    Key output                  Gate
1 Discovery      2-3     Sponsor              Findings + equity table     Findings accepted
2 Strategy       2       Sponsor + founders   Strategy + creative brief   Brief signed
3 Exploration    2-3     Decision group       2-3 territories → 1         Direction chosen
4 Development    3-4     Brand owner          Logo system, color, type…   Core identity approved
5 Validation     2       Legal + brand owner  Searches, accessibility,    Go / fix
                                              customer feedback, tests
6 System         2-4     Brand owner          Guidelines, templates,      Toolkit handed over
                                              tokens, asset packs
7 Rollout        4-12+   Project lead         Launch, training, phased    Launch KPIs reviewed
                                              replacement
Budget lines: design · research · legal/trademark · fonts/licenses · photography ·
              production (print, signage) · web changes · training · contingency (10-15%)
```

(Durations are illustrative for a small-to-mid-size brand; compress or extend to fit.)

### Validation checklist before launch

```text
[ ] Trademark clearance in each market and class (attorney for key brands)
[ ] Domain, social handles and app-store names available or secured
[ ] Accessibility: pairings matrix passes WCAG 2.2 AA; logo legible at 16 px
[ ] Scripts: Arabic/Urdu lockups reviewed by native readers
[ ] Unintended meanings checked in all target languages/markets
[ ] Application tests: app icon, avatar, signage, packaging proof, dark mode
[ ] Customer feedback on comprehension and fit (not "do you like it?")
[ ] Ownership: copyright assignment, font licenses, image rights
```

### Presentation outline (seven parts)

1. What we heard (research and equity)
2. The strategy (positioning and personality)
3. The idea (one sentence)
4. The identity core (logo system, color, type)
5. The system in action (applications and mockups)
6. What we keep and why
7. Rollout and next steps

### Summary

Run the rebrand in phases, manage stakeholders deliberately, present strategy before visuals and show the system in use, handle feedback against the brief, and validate legally, culturally and practically before launch.

scenes.narration: Here's something that surprises designers who lead their first rebrand. The design work is often the easy part. The hard parts are getting ten stakeholders to agree, discovering a trademark conflict two weeks before launch, handling a CEO who sees the work for the first time at the final meeting, and replacing a logo on four hundred items. A rebrand is a change-management project with a design at its center. In this lecture, you'll learn the seven phases of a rebrand, how to manage stakeholders, how to present identity work, how to handle feedback, what to validate before launch, and how to plan timelines and budgets. By the end, you'll be able to run a rebrand like a project, not a guessing game.

Without phases, decision points and clear owners, you get endless revisions, late surprises and budget overruns. Think of building an extension on a house. There are plans, permits, inspections, a schedule and a budget. Nobody starts laying bricks before the permit is approved. Rebrands need the same discipline: each phase ends with a decision gate, and you don't move on until the right people have agreed.

lessons.title: Rolling out a new identity
lessons.body:
### Launch is the beginning, not the end

A new identity only works when it appears correctly across every touchpoint. Rollout is where many rebrands falter: old logos linger for years, teams use outdated templates, and customers are confused by mixed signals.

### Plan the rollout

**1. Inventory every touchpoint.** Use the audit from discovery and add everything physical and digital:

```
Touchpoint inventory (sample)
Digital:  website, app icon, favicon, social avatars/banners, email templates,
          signatures, ad accounts, marketplace listings, map listings, payment pages
Documents: proposals, decks, invoices, contracts, reports
Physical: signage, packaging, labels, vehicles, uniforms, stationery, merch
Partners: reseller materials, directory listings, sponsor listings
```

**2. Prioritize.** Score each by visibility, cost and lead time.

| Priority | Examples |
|---|---|
| Launch day | Website, social profiles, email signatures, templates, key ads |
| First month | Proposals, decks, invoices, marketplace listings, partner kits |
| Phased / natural replacement | Packaging (when stock runs out), uniforms, vehicles, signage (budget permitting) |

**3. Choose a rollout approach:**

- **Big bang** — everything changes on one day. High impact, high cost, high coordination. Suits small digital-first brands.
- **Phased** — digital first, physical over time. Most common for small businesses.
- **Natural replacement** — replace items as they wear out or run out. Cheapest but slowest; risks long periods of mixed identity.

Many brands combine: big bang for digital, phased for physical.

### Communicate the change

Customers should understand that it is still the same business:

- **Announcement post or video** explaining why (growth, new services, better experience), showing old and new.
- **Transition cues:** for a period, "formerly X" or keeping a familiar color helps recognition.
- **Customer-facing staff briefing:** what changed, why, how to answer questions.
- **Search and listings:** update business names and logos on map listings, directories and marketplaces; keep redirects if domains change.
- **For creators:** tell followers before changing handles or channel names; platforms may limit how often names can change, and changes can break links or confuse followers.

### Internal launch and training

- Share the story and the toolkit.
- Run a short training session and provide a recorded version.
- Remove old templates and logo files from shared drives (archive them, with clear labels).
- Set a date after which old materials must not be used.

### Measuring the rollout

Track:

- **Completion:** percentage of touchpoints updated by priority.
- **Consistency:** audit samples after 30 and 90 days.
- **Audience response:** comments, customer feedback, and sales team observations.
- **Business signals** tied to original objectives: enquiry quality, conversion rates, average deal size, retention — interpreted carefully, since many factors affect them.

Avoid over-reacting to early negative comments; audiences often need time to adjust. Distinguish between genuine usability problems (fix them) and unfamiliarity (give it time).

### Worked example: a café chain's phased rollout

- **Launch week:** new website, social profiles, delivery-app listings, menus (digital), staff email signatures; announcement post "Same coffee, new look" showing old vs new.
- **Month 1:** printed menus, loyalty cards, takeaway cups (new stock ordered), partner kits for delivery platforms.
- **Months 2–6:** exterior signage per branch as budget allows, uniforms replaced at scheduled renewal.
- **Measurement:** checklist completion per branch; audit at 90 days found two branches using old menu templates — fixed and old files archived.

### Common mistakes

- No touchpoint inventory, so old assets linger.
- Announcing a rebrand without explaining why.
- Leaving old templates accessible.
- Judging success in the first week.

### Handling handles, domains and search

Digital identity changes need special care. If a domain changes, set up permanent redirects from old pages to new ones so links and search visibility are preserved, and update the business name on listings consistently. If social handles change, reserve the new handles early, consider keeping the old handle as a placeholder where platforms allow, and update links in bios, email signatures and printed materials. For creators, pin a short explanation to the profile for a few weeks so returning followers know they are in the right place.

### Hands-on: touchpoint inventory with priority scores

```text
TOUCHPOINT INVENTORY — score 1-3 each; priority = visibility × (4 - lead time)
Touchpoint               Owner     Visibility  Lead time  Cost   Priority  Target date
Website + favicon        Web       3           1          2      9         Launch day
Instagram/TikTok/LinkedIn Social   3           1          1      9         Launch day
Google Business Profile  Ops       3           1          1      9         Launch day
Email signatures         IT        2           1          1      6         Launch day
Proposal/invoice templates Finance 2           1          1      6         Week 2
Marketplace listings     E-com     2           2          1      4         Week 3
Packaging                Ops       3           3          3      3         Next stock run
Shop signage             Ops       3           3          3      3         Month 3
Uniforms / vehicles      Ops       2           3          3      2         Natural replacement
```

(Scores are illustrative; the formula is a simple way to rank — adapt it.)

### Digital housekeeping on launch day

- **Handles and names:** update display names first; change handles only if the old one is kept or redirected, because some platforms free old handles for others to claim.
- **Website and search:** if the domain changes, set up permanent (301) redirects from every old URL to its new equivalent, update the site in Google Search Console, and refresh structured data and social preview images.
- **Listings:** update Google Business Profile, map listings, app stores, marketplaces and directories — consistency of name, logo and details matters for customers and local search.
- **Email and documents:** signatures, templates and auto-replies ("We've changed our look — same team").

### Measuring the rollout

| Metric | How |
|---|---|
| Touchpoint completion | % of inventory items updated by target date |
| Consistency | Brand audit score (from governance) at 30 and 90 days |
| Customer understanding | Comments, support questions, short survey on recognition |
| Search and traffic continuity | Branded search and site traffic vs pre-launch baseline |
| Adoption | Template usage vs files built from scratch |

### Before/after: a café chain's phased rollout

| | Before (big-bang attempt) | After (phased) |
|---|---|---|
| Launch day | Tried to change everything; missed half of it | Digital, menus and staff badges only |
| Packaging | Destroyed old stock early | Old cups used up; new cups from the next order |
| Customers | Confused by mixed signage for months | Clear announcement: "Same café, fresh look" + in-store cards |

### Summary

Inventory and prioritize every touchpoint, choose a rollout approach, communicate clearly to customers and staff, remove old assets, and measure completion, consistency and response over time.

scenes.narration: Here's a strange sight you've probably seen. A brand launches a shiny new identity, and two years later, you still find the old logo on a delivery van, a forgotten web page, a map listing and the back of a menu. Mixed signals like that confuse customers and quietly erode the investment. Launch day isn't the finish line. It's the start of the rollout. In this lecture, you'll learn how to inventory and prioritize every touchpoint, choose a rollout approach, communicate the change to customers and staff, handle handles, domains and search, and measure whether the rollout worked. By the end, you'll have a rollout plan that actually gets finished.

Printing, signage, packaging, uniforms and web changes often cost more than the design itself. Think of moving house. Designing the new home is exciting, but if you don't update your address with the bank, the post office and your friends, mail keeps going to the old place for years.
